records.title: Celestial phenomenon over Nuremberg
records.place: Nuremberg, Holy Roman Empire (Germany)
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Usually interpreted as a spectacular sun-halo display (parhelia, arcs) described in religious terms.
records.shape: Spheres, crosses, tubes and a black spear
records.witnesses: Citizens of Nuremberg
records.summary: A broadsheet by Hans Glaser describes a dawn "battle" in the sky: globes, crosses and cylinders that moved and fought before falling to the ground with smoke. It is a staple of UFO histories and an example of how atmospheric optics were recorded before modern science.

timeline.text: Objects seen near the rising sun; broadsheet printed afterwards.

records.title: Celestial phenomenon over Basel
records.place: Basel, Swiss Confederacy (Switzerland)
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Generally read as atmospheric optics (sun halos, a reddened rising sun) or dust and smoke, described in the religious language of a 16th-century broadsheet.
records.shape: Many black and fiery spheres
records.witnesses: Townspeople of Basel (as reported by the broadsheet)
records.summary: A broadsheet printed in Basel by Samuel Coccius reported that at sunrise on August 7, 1566 many large black spheres were seen racing toward the Sun and seeming to fight one another, some turning red and fiery before fading. It also described a blood-red Sun on the mornings and evenings of late July. Together with Nuremberg 1561, it is one of the best-known early-modern "sky battles".

timeline.text: Broadsheet reports the Sun rising and setting blood-red, with a dark disc in front of it.
Many large black spheres are seen moving at speed before the Sun, some turning fiery.
Samuel Coccius publishes the account as a warning sign from God.

records.title: Utsuro-bune — the "hollow ship" of Hitachi
records.place: Haratono-hama, Hitachi Province (Ibaraki), Japan
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Historians treat it as folklore: the story appears in several Edo-period collections with conflicting details, and resembles older legends of exiled women set adrift in boats.
records.shape: Round vessel of wood and iron with glass windows
records.witnesses: Fishermen (as told in Edo-period accounts)
records.summary: Several Japanese books of the 1820s–1840s tell how fishermen found a strange round boat washed up on the coast of Hitachi Province in 1803. Inside was a young woman who spoke no known language and clutched a box she would let no one touch. The fishermen pushed the vessel back out to sea. The drawings of the round, windowed ship are often compared with modern "flying saucers".

timeline.text: A round vessel drifts ashore at Haratono-hama (date as given in the accounts).
Story published in Tōen shōsetsu, with an illustration.
Further versions appear in Ume-no-chiri and other collections.

records.title: Bonilla observation — objects crossing the Sun
records.place: Zacatecas Astronomical Observatory, Mexico
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Camille Flammarion thought Bonilla had seen birds, insects or dust close to the telescope. A 2011 study at UNAM proposed fragments of a comet passing close to Earth. Either way, nothing suggests craft.
records.shape: Hundreds of dark, fuzzy bodies with tails
records.witnesses: 1 astronomer (José Bonilla)
records.summary: On August 12, 1883, José Bonilla, the first director of the Zacatecas observatory, was preparing to observe sunspots when he saw dark objects crossing the face of the Sun. Over two days he counted hundreds of them and took photographs through the telescope. They were published in L'Astronomie in 1886 and are often called the first photographs of unidentified flying objects.

timeline.text: Bonilla sees objects crossing the solar disc and begins counting and photographing.
Objects are still seen crossing the Sun.
Flammarion publishes the report and a photograph in L'Astronomie.
UNAM researchers propose a fragmenting comet passing a few hundred km from Earth.

records.title: Mystery airship wave
records.place: California to the Midwest and Texas, United States
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: No powered airship capable of such flights existed. Reports are attributed to newspaper hoaxes (some papers invented stories outright), bright planets such as Venus, hot-air "fire balloons" and pranks.
records.shape: Cigar-shaped "airship" with lights and wings or propellers
records.witnesses: Thousands, over five months
records.summary: In November 1896 people in Sacramento and then San Francisco and Oakland reported a lighted airship moving across the night sky. In early 1897 reports spread east through Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa, Illinois and Texas, often with tall tales of inventors and crews. The line on the map joins the main clusters of reports in date order. It is a wave of sightings, not one object.

timeline.text: Hundreds in Sacramento report a light moving against the wind.
Reports over Oakland and San Francisco; the San Francisco Call prints drawings.
Sightings begin in Nebraska around Hastings and Omaha.
Peak across Kansas, Missouri, Iowa and Illinois; Chicago crowds watch on Apr 9–10.
The Aurora, Texas "crash" story ends the wave.

records.title: Aurora, Texas airship "crash"
records.place: Aurora, Wise County, Texas
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Widely regarded as a newspaper hoax written to draw attention to a town in decline. Later digs, metal samples and a search of the cemetery found nothing unusual.
records.shape: Airship
records.witnesses: Newspaper account by S. E. Haydon
records.summary: On April 19, 1897 the Dallas Morning News printed a report from Aurora. It said an airship had struck Judge J. S. Proctor's windmill around 6 a.m. and exploded, and that the pilot, "not an inhabitant of this world", had been buried in the town cemetery. It came at the very end of the 1896–97 airship wave and has been re-investigated many times since the 1970s.

timeline.text: Airship said to hit a windmill on the Proctor farm and explode.
Dallas Morning News publishes S. E. Haydon's report.
Renewed interest; investigators search the cemetery and the well site.

records.title: Tunguska explosion
records.place: Podkamennaya Tunguska River basin, Central Siberia
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The scientific consensus is the air burst of a stony asteroid or a comet fragment tens of metres across, which exploded some 5 to 14 km above the taiga and left no crater. The idea that an alien spacecraft blew up there began with Alexander Kazantsev’s 1946 science-fiction story “Explosion” and has no physical support.
records.shape: A fiery body crossing the sky, “a second sun”, then a blinding flash and blast
records.witnesses: Evenk herders and settlers; the trading post at Vanavara, about 60 km away
records.duration: Seconds; the blast was heard hundreds of kilometres away
records.summary: At about 7:14 a.m. local time on June 30, 1908, a fireball crossed the sky over Central Siberia and exploded above the forest near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River. At the Vanavara trading post, about 60 km to the south, Semyon Semyonov later recalled that “the sky was split in two” and that the heat and the blast threw him off the porch. Seismographs as far away as Irkutsk, Tashkent, Tiflis and Jena recorded the shock, and the night skies over Europe and Asia glowed for days. About 2,150 km² of forest, several million trees, were flattened in a radial pattern, but Leonid Kulik’s expeditions, which reached the centre in 1927, found no crater: at the middle the trees still stood, stripped of their branches. The event is explained as the air burst of a small asteroid or comet; the “exploding spaceship” owes its life to a science-fiction story written in 1946.

timeline.text: A fireball crosses the sky and explodes above the taiga; seismographs across Eurasia record the shock.
Bright night skies are reported across Europe and Asia.
Leonid Kulik leads the first scientific survey of the region.
Kulik reaches the centre: flattened forest in a radial pattern, standing stripped trees, no crater.
Alexander Kazantsev’s story “Explosion” proposes a nuclear-powered alien ship.
Computer models favour a stony body 50–80 m across bursting 10–14 km up.

points.note: Enters the atmosphere from the east-south-east

sources.label: Wikipedia — Tunguska event

records.title: The 1909 New Zealand airship scare
records.place: Kelso, West Otago, and across the South Island, New Zealand
records.explanation: There was no airship in New Zealand in 1909. Most of the reports were of lights at night; the meteorologist Clement Wragge suggested secret local trials or “cosmic dust”, and said some observers had mistaken Venus, Jupiter and Mars for an airship, while others blamed hoaxers, kite lanterns and fire balloons. Historians treat it as one of the “scareship” panics of 1909–1913, when newspapers in Britain, Australia and New Zealand were full of fears of foreign airships. The daylight “boat” seen at Kelso has no specific explanation.
records.shape: A boat- or cigar-shaped craft by day; a moving light, sometimes with a searchlight, by night
records.witnesses: Schoolchildren and at least five adults at Kelso; residents of Dunedin, Christchurch, Oamaru, Orepuki and Blenheim; a bar pilot at the Wairau Bar
records.duration: Weeks: reports ran from mid-July into early September 1909
records.summary: In the last weeks of July 1909 the South Island’s newspapers began to fill with reports of a mysterious “airship”. At Kelso in West Otago, children at the school said that around noon a boat-shaped machine, pointed at both ends, with a short mast and what looked like a man sitting in it, flew over the school grounds, turned and went back toward the Blue Mountains; the local correspondent wrote that at least five people had seen it and their accounts agreed. At night, lights were reported from Orepuki, Oamaru, Christchurch and Dunedin, where a man woken at 2 a.m. said he saw a large dark object with a searchlight float past Knox College. In Blenheim on July 31 a crowd at the Criterion Hotel corner watched a light toward the Wairau Bar until after midnight, and a bar pilot reported a light passing over the pilot station toward Kaikōura. No airship existed in the country, and the reports faded by September.

timeline.text: Reports of strange lights begin in Otago and Southland.
Kelso schoolchildren and adults describe a boat-shaped craft circling the school.
A Dunedin man reports a dark object with a searchlight passing Knox College at 2 a.m.
A crowd in Blenheim watches a light over the Wairau Bar until after midnight.
Clement Wragge attributes the lights to planets and cosmic dust.
The reports die away.

sources.label: Otago Daily Times, “100 years ago”: the Kelso report of July 1909
Marlborough Express, August 2, 1909, “Seen in Blenheim” (transcription)
Gisborne Times, August 6, 1909 (Papers Past)

records.title: The Sheerness airship — questions in Parliament
records.place: Sheerness and Queenborough, Isle of Sheppey, Kent
records.explanation: Never identified. Churchill told the Commons only that it was “not one of our own airships”, and privately that there was “very little doubt” it was German; the German naval Zeppelin L 1, the likeliest candidate, had landed near Berlin three hours earlier, and Germany denied any flight. The historian Brett Holman thinks an unrecorded British night flight at least as likely.
records.shape: An engine heard overhead; some saw a red light and perhaps a searchlight
records.witnesses: Townspeople of Sheerness and Queenborough, among them a Royal Navy lieutenant; the naval air station at Eastchurch
records.summary: Between about 6:30 and 7 p.m. on October 14, 1912, people in Sheerness, the naval dockyard town at the mouth of the Medway, heard what sounded like an aircraft engine overhead, and some, a Royal Navy lieutenant among them, thought they saw a red light moving over the town. The naval air station at Eastchurch heard the engine too and lit flares for it, but nothing landed. A month later questions in the House of Commons asked about a “Zeppelin dirigible” over Sheerness, and on November 27 Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty, confirmed that an unknown aircraft had been heard but said he could not tell its nationality, only that it was not a British airship. The conservative press read it as a German reconnaissance flight, and the episode set off the “phantom airship” scare of early 1913, when lights and engines were reported across Britain. No German airship was ever shown to have made the flight.

timeline.text: An engine is heard over Sheerness; a red light is seen moving over the town.
Eastchurch lights flares; the sound fades and nothing lands.
The Admiralty asks the captain of HMS Actaeon for a report.
William Joynson-Hicks asks in the Commons about a Zeppelin over Sheerness.
Churchill: an unknown aircraft was heard; it was “not one of our own airships”.
The phantom airship scare spreads across Britain.

sources.label: Hansard — House of Commons, 27 November 1912
Brett Holman — The Sheerness incident (Airminded)

records.title: Great Meteor Procession
records.place: Toronto, Ontario, on a path from Saskatchewan to Bermuda
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The astronomer Clarence Chant collected more than a hundred reports and found they all lay along one great-circle arc, with no radiant. He concluded the fireballs were the pieces of a small, short-lived natural satellite of the Earth, breaking up as it grazed the atmosphere. Later studies by John O’Keefe and others agreed.
records.shape: A procession of 40 to 60 slow fireballs in groups, with a bright tail-less body at the rear
records.witnesses: More than a hundred reports from Canada, the northeastern United States, Bermuda and ships at sea
records.duration: Each fireball 30–40 seconds; the whole procession about five minutes
records.summary: At about 9 p.m. on February 9, 1913, people across Canada and the northeastern United States saw between 40 and 60 bright, slow fireballs cross the sky from horizon to horizon on practically the same path. They came in groups, threw out sparks and were followed by a clear, tail-less light “like a big star”; some witnesses heard rumbling. The same procession was reported from Bermuda and from ships as far south as Brazil, a ground track of more than 11,000 km. Much of the populous Northeast was under cloud, so most of the reports came from rural Canada. From the sound reports William Pickering put the meteors at about 56 km up. O’Keefe later named them the Cyrillids, after the feast day of St. Cyril of Alexandria, February 9.

timeline.text: The first fireballs are reported over Saskatchewan and move east-south-east.
The procession passes over Ontario: 40 to 60 fireballs in groups, each visible 30 to 40 seconds.
The last, tail-less body passes; observers in New York and Pennsylvania hear thunder-like noise.
Observers on Bermuda see the leading bodies “like large arc lights … slightly violet”.
Clarence Chant publishes his analysis in the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada.

points.note: North of Escanaba, Michigan, seen low in the north
Over southern Ontario, about 56 km up
Seen from Bermuda; ships report it farther south

sources.label: Wikipedia — 1913 Great Meteor Procession

records.title: Brown Mountain lights
records.place: Brown Mountain, Pisgah National Forest, North Carolina
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: In 1922, U.S. Geological Survey geologist George R. Mansfield used maps and an alidade to show the lights were train headlights, car headlights and brush fires in the valleys beyond the ridge. A 1913 USGS look had already pointed to locomotive headlights.
records.shape: Lights rising above the ridge
records.witnesses: Visitors to overlooks such as Wiseman's View
records.summary: In 1913 the Charlotte Observer reported lights rising over Brown Mountain in the Blue Ridge, during the years when electric lighting and railways were reaching the area. Two U.S. Geological Survey investigations followed. Legends of lights "seen by the Cherokee" were added later. The lights are still watched from roadside overlooks.

timeline.text: Charlotte Observer publishes reports of the lights.
USGS look: locomotive headlights.
USGS geologist George Mansfield: trains, cars and brush fires.

records.title: The South African “phantom monoplane”
records.place: Across the Union of South Africa: the Transvaal, Natal, the Cape and the Free State
records.explanation: At the time it was taken for a German monoplane from South-West Africa on a spy or bombing mission, but the distances from German territory made that unlikely, and no aircraft was ever found. The sociologist Robert Bartholomew studied the episode in 1989 as a case of collective delusion: a war scare in the weeks before the South-West Africa campaign, in which lights in the night sky were read as the lamps of an enemy aircraft.
records.shape: A monoplane, or its headlights, seen at night and said to manoeuvre
records.witnesses: Thousands of people, reported in dozens of articles in the Rand Daily Mail, the Star, the Cape Times, the Cape Argus, the Natal Advertiser and the Pretoria News
records.duration: About a month, August 11 to September 9, 1914
records.summary: In the first weeks of the First World War, with South Africa about to invade German South-West Africa, people across the country began to report a monoplane flying at night, sometimes with headlights, sometimes circling or hovering. The sightings came from towns hundreds of kilometres apart and from every province, and newspapers printed dozens of reports between August 11 and September 9, 1914. Many readers assumed a German machine was spying or preparing to bomb; no aircraft was ever found, and the scare ended as suddenly as it began. It is now cited, with the airship scares of the same years, as a classic example of how a war scare turns ordinary night lights into enemy aircraft.

timeline.text: Britain, and with it South Africa, is at war with Germany.
The first monoplane reports appear.
Reports come from all four provinces; a German spy plane is widely suspected.
The last reports; no aircraft is found.
Robert Bartholomew analyses the episode as mass hysteria.

sources.label: Bartholomew, “The South African Monoplane Hysteria”, Sociological Inquiry 59 (1989)
Wikipedia — UFO sightings in South Africa

records.title: Fátima — the “miracle of the sun”
records.place: Cova da Iria, near Fátima, Portugal
records.explanation: The Catholic Church declared the apparitions “worthy of belief” in 1930. Scientists point to the effects of staring at the Sun through thinning cloud (after-images, bleached photoreceptors and the illusion of movement), perhaps helped by high dust or a sundog, and to a crowd that had been told to expect a sign. Some ufologists have reinterpreted it as a UFO event; nothing was seen in the sky by observatories, or by people away from the crowd.
records.shape: The Sun as a dull, spinning silver disc, casting coloured light and seeming to plunge towards the earth
records.witnesses: A crowd usually estimated at 50,000 to 70,000, including journalists such as Avelino de Almeida of O Século
records.summary: Three shepherd children had said that a lady who appeared to them at the Cova da Iria would perform a miracle at noon on October 13, 1917. A crowd of tens of thousands gathered in heavy rain; early in the afternoon, around solar noon, the clouds parted and many in the crowd reported that the Sun became a dull disc that could be looked at, spun, threw off coloured light, zig-zagged and seemed to fall towards them before returning to its place, and that their soaked clothes dried at once. Newspaper accounts, including the anticlerical O Século, described the crowd’s reaction; not everyone present saw the Sun move, and no astronomical observatory recorded anything unusual. The Church recognised the apparitions in 1930. Physicists and sceptics explain the sight as what the eye does when it stares at the Sun, with suggestion doing the rest.

timeline.text: The children report monthly apparitions and announce a miracle for October 13.
The rain stops and the clouds open; the crowd sees the Sun “dance” for about ten minutes.
O Século and other papers publish eyewitness accounts.
Ilustração Portuguesa prints Judah Ruah’s photographs of the crowd.
The Bishop of Leiria declares the apparitions worthy of belief.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Miracle of the Sun

records.title: Battle of Los Angeles
records.place: Los Angeles, California
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The Navy attributed the alarm to "war nerves" after a Japanese submarine shelled the Ellwood oil field the night before; a weather balloon is thought to have started the barrage. The famous Los Angeles Times photo was heavily retouched.
records.shape: Unidentified targets / searchlight cone
records.witnesses: Thousands; coastal anti-aircraft batteries
records.duration: About 2 hours, with the barrage lasting about 1 hour
records.summary: Less than three months after Pearl Harbor, radar and observers reported an unidentified target approaching Los Angeles. Anti-aircraft batteries fired more than 1,400 shells into the night sky while searchlights converged over Santa Monica and Culver City. No aircraft was downed and no bombs fell; falling shrapnel and heart attacks caused deaths on the ground.

timeline.text: Warning issued the evening before after the Ellwood submarine attack.
Radar picks up a target about 120 miles west of Los Angeles; blackout ordered.
37th Coast Artillery Brigade opens fire; barrage continues for about an hour.
All-clear sounded; no wreckage is ever found.

points.note: Radar contact ~120 mi west of the city
Searchlights pick up object off Santa Monica
Barrage centred over Santa Monica / Culver City
Reports of targets moving toward Long Beach

records.title: Foo fighters — 415th Night Fighter Squadron
records.place: Rhine valley near Strasbourg
records.explanation: Proposed explanations include St. Elmo’s fire, ball lightning, flares and misidentified aircraft; none fits all reports.
records.shape: Balls of orange or red light pacing aircraft
records.witnesses: USAAF night-fighter crews
records.summary: Crews of the U.S. 415th Night Fighter Squadron repeatedly reported glowing balls of light that followed their Beaufighters over the Rhine. They called them "foo fighters"; similar reports came from Allied and Axis crews in Europe and the Pacific.

timeline.text: Lt. Edward Schlueter’s crew reports 8–10 orange lights.
Reports continue; press coins "foo fighters".

records.title: The Trinity crash story
records.place: The Padilla ranch near San Antonio, New Mexico, north-west of the Trinity test site
records.explanation: Nothing but the two men’s account supports it, and it was first told 58 years later. The skeptic Brian Dunning (Skeptoid, 2024) called it “a literal hoax”: Reme Baca pitched several versions to UFO authors, no one corroborates it, and the state policeman said to have looked at the wreck was reportedly in Europe with the Army at the time. Jacques Vallée and Paola Harris, who published the story in 2021, consider it genuine. The “souvenir” the men say they kept has not been analysed by any laboratory.
records.shape: An avocado-shaped metal craft with a transparent dome
records.witnesses: Reme Baca and Jose Padilla, then aged 7 and 9 (by their account)
records.duration: An afternoon, then days of recovery work they say they watched
records.summary: In 2003 two New Mexico men told a reporter of the Socorro Mountain Mail that on August 16, 1945, a month after the first atomic test, they had seen an object crash on the Padilla family ranch near San Antonio. In their telling the boys, 7 and 9, found a damaged avocado-shaped craft with a transparent dome and small creatures inside, “similar to a praying mantis, or a Jerusalem cricket, with pear-shaped heads”. The military took the wreck away and the family was told it was a weather balloon. The men self-published a memoir in 2011, and in 2021 Jacques Vallée and Paola Harris made it the subject of Trinity: The Best-Kept Secret, arguing that it was an earlier Roswell. Critics point out that the story surfaced only decades later, changed between tellings and has no independent witness or record.

timeline.text: The Trinity test, some 40 km south-east of the ranch.
The date the two men give for the crash.
The story first appears, in the Mountain Mail of Socorro.
Baca and Padilla self-publish Born on the Edge of Ground Zero.
Vallée and Harris publish Trinity: The Best-Kept Secret.
Skeptoid calls the story a hoax.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Trinity UFO Case
Brian Dunning, Skeptoid #929, “The Trinity UFO Crash”

records.title: Ängelholm landing report
records.place: Kronoskogen, Ängelholm, Sweden
records.explanation: There is only one witness, and his account grew over the years. The traces he pointed to were never independently documented, and the story is not corroborated.
records.shape: Disc landed in a forest clearing
records.witnesses: 1 (Gösta Carlsson)
records.summary: Businessman Gösta Carlsson said that in May 1946, during the Swedish ghost-rocket summer, he came upon a disc-shaped craft standing in a clearing in the Kronoskogen forest and was warned off by its occupants. In 1972 he built a small memorial at the spot, marking where he said the craft had stood. It is now a local landmark.

timeline.text: Carlsson says he saw a landed craft and occupants in a clearing.
Carlsson first tells the story in public, in an interview with a journalist.
Carlsson erects a memorial marking the landing marks he described.
His account is published in book form and grows in detail.

records.title: Ghost rockets — Lake Kölmjärv
records.place: Lake Kölmjärv, Norrbotten, Sweden
records.explanation: Swedish, British and U.S. investigators found no Soviet rockets; many of ~2,000 reports were meteors, but around 200 radar returns and several crashes into lakes were never explained.
records.shape: Rocket- or cigar-shaped objects
records.witnesses: Farmer Knut Lindbäck and others; Swedish military
records.summary: During 1946 Scandinavian observers logged about 2,000 sightings of rocket-like objects. On 19 July a farmer watched one plunge into Lake Kölmjärv; the Swedish Army searched the lake for two weeks and found only a fresh crater in the lakebed.

timeline.text: First reports from Finland.
Object crashes into Lake Kölmjärv.
Peak of sightings (coincides with the Perseids).

records.title: Maury Island incident
records.place: Maury Island, Puget Sound, Washington
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Investigators judged it a hoax: the “debris” was ordinary slag and rock, and the photographs showed nothing. The two men involved later gave conflicting accounts.
records.shape: Six doughnut-shaped craft, one said to be damaged
records.witnesses: Harold Dahl, his son and a colleague, Fred Crisman (claimed)
records.summary: A harbour patrolman, Harold Dahl, said six large doughnut-shaped craft circled above his boat off Maury Island in the afternoon of June 21, 1947, three days before Kenneth Arnold’s famous sighting. One craft was said to be damaged and to shed hot metallic slag that burned his son and killed the dog. Dahl’s employer, Fred Crisman, backed the story, and the case was investigated by Kenneth Arnold and by two Army Air Forces intelligence officers. It is remembered as one of the first reported UFO hoaxes, and for the first story of a “man in black” silencing a witness.

timeline.text: Dahl reports six doughnut-shaped craft over Puget Sound, one dropping slag.
A man in a dark suit is said to warn Dahl not to talk: the first “man in black” story.
Arnold and two Army Air Forces officers interview Dahl and Crisman in Tacoma.
The officers’ B-25 crashes near Kelso, Washington, on the way back to California; both die.
The “fragments” are found to be slag and rock; the case is written off as a hoax.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Maury Island incident

records.title: Kenneth Arnold — "flying saucers" over Mount Rainier
records.place: Mount Rainier, Washington
records.explanation: Project Blue Book listed the sighting as a mirage. Other proposals include a fireball, pelicans and reflections; none has been widely accepted.
records.shape: Nine thin, crescent / convex objects in echelon
records.witnesses: 1 pilot (Kenneth Arnold)
records.summary: Private pilot Kenneth Arnold, searching for a crashed Marine C-46 in his CallAir A-2, saw nine bright objects in a chain flying south past Mount Rainier. He timed them from Rainier to Mount Adams — roughly 50 miles — in 1 minute 42 seconds, implying well over 1,200 mph. The press coverage coined "flying saucer" and began the modern UFO era.

timeline.text: Near Mineral, WA at 9,200 ft, Arnold sees a bright flash to the north.
Nine objects in echelon pass in front of Mount Rainier heading south.
Objects fade from view near Mount Adams; 1 min 42 s after passing Rainier.
Arnold tells reporters at the East Oregonian in Pendleton; story goes national.

points.note: Passing in front of Mount Rainier
Faded from view near Mount Adams
Turns south on a parallel course

records.title: Rhodes photographs — Phoenix
records.place: Phoenix, Arizona
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The Air Force file records that Dr. Irving Langmuir, told a thunderstorm had just passed, judged the object to be paper carried up by the wind; photographers it consulted doubted the pictures. A historian has since argued they were faked.
records.shape: Heel-shaped disc with a hole in the centre
records.witnesses: 1 (William A. Rhodes)
records.summary: Amateur astronomer and inventor William Rhodes said he heard a "whoosh" like a jet, grabbed his camera and took two photographs of a heel-shaped object circling over his home. The Arizona Republic printed them on July 9, 1947. The FBI and Army counter-intelligence took the negatives, and the case became "Incident 40" in the Air Force files, one of the first UFO photographs to be studied officially.

timeline.text: Rhodes hears a loud "whoosh" and takes two photographs.
The Arizona Republic runs the photos on the front page.
FBI and Army CIC interview Rhodes and take the prints and negatives.
The photos appear in the Air Force's first secret UFO study.

points.note: Spirals down to about 2,000 ft; photographed

records.title: Roswell debris recovery
records.place: Foster homestead near Corona, New Mexico
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The U.S. Air Force reports of 1994–1997 identified the debris as a Project Mogul balloon train (NYU Flight 4) launched from Alamogordo Army Air Field to listen for Soviet nuclear tests, and later "alien body" stories as conflations with 1950s dummy drops.
records.shape: Debris of foil, rubber, sticks and tape
records.witnesses: Rancher Mac Brazel; 509th Bomb Group officers
records.summary: Rancher W. W. "Mac" Brazel found a field of debris on the Foster ranch. On July 8, 1947, Roswell Army Air Field announced it had recovered a "flying disc"; within a day the Army re-described it as a weather balloon. Interest revived in the late 1970s, and the Air Force published two reports concluding the debris came from Project Mogul.

timeline.text: Project Mogul Flight 4 launched from Alamogordo Army Air Field (per USAF reconstruction).
Brazel finds debris on the Foster homestead.
RAAF press release: "flying disc" recovered; Fort Worth then shows balloon debris.
USAF reports attribute the debris to Project Mogul.

points.note: Last tracked in the Arabela–Corona area
Debris field on the Foster homestead

records.title: Mantell UFO incident
records.place: Godman Field, Fort Knox, Kentucky
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Project Blue Book (Ruppelt) concluded Mantell was most likely chasing a classified Navy Skyhook balloon, probably launched from Clinton County AFB, Ohio. Mantell climbed above 25,000 ft without oxygen and lost consciousness.
records.shape: Large bright object, "ice-cream cone" / metallic
records.witnesses: Godman tower staff, police, 4 P-51 pilots
records.summary: Kentucky Highway Patrol reports of a large circular object near Maysville reached Godman Field, where tower staff saw it too. A flight of four Kentucky Air National Guard P-51 Mustangs was asked to investigate. Capt. Thomas Mantell kept climbing after his wingmen levelled off, blacked out without oxygen and died when his P-51 crashed on a farm south of Franklin.

timeline.text: Highway Patrol reports an object near Maysville moving west.
Godman tower operators see the object.
Four P-51s diverted; Mantell climbs toward it.
Mantell passes 25,000 ft; last transmissions.
Crash reported south of Franklin, KY.

points.note: Wingmen level off; Mantell keeps climbing
Above 25,000 ft without oxygen — blacks out
Crash site south of Franklin, KY

records.title: Aztec “crashed saucer” — the story that ended in a fraud trial
records.place: Hart Canyon, about 12 miles north-east of Aztec, New Mexico (as the story told it)
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: A hoax. The story came from two confidence men, Silas Newton and Leo GeBauer, who used it to sell “doodlebug” oil-finding devices said to be built on saucer technology. The journalist J. P. Cahn exposed it in True magazine in 1952 (their “alien metal” was ordinary aluminium), and both men were convicted of fraud in 1953. No contemporary record of a crash or a recovery exists, and the local sheriff, newspaper editor and landowners denied that anything happened.
records.shape: A disc 99 feet across with sixteen small bodies inside, according to the story
records.witnesses: None independent: the account came from Newton and GeBauer through Frank Scully
records.summary: In 1949 the Variety columnist Frank Scully told his readers, and in 1950 the buyers of his best-seller Behind the Flying Saucers, that in March 1948 the military had recovered a 99-foot disc with sixteen small humanoid bodies after it landed in Hart Canyon, north-east of Aztec, New Mexico. His sources were Silas Newton, an oil promoter, and a “Dr. Gee”, Leo GeBauer, who were selling devices they said could find oil because they used technology from the saucer. In 1952 the San Francisco Chronicle reporter J. P. Cahn obtained a sample of their “saucer metal”, had it tested and found ordinary aluminium; his True magazine article exposed the scheme, and one of their victims pressed charges. Newton and GeBauer were convicted of fraud in 1953. The story was dropped for twenty years, then revived from the 1970s by writers who dated the crash to March 25, 1948; a 1950 FBI memo by Guy Hottel, about three saucers said to have been recovered in New Mexico, is often tied to it, but the FBI calls it an uninvestigated second- or third-hand claim. It belongs here as one of the first “crashed saucer” stories, and one of the few that ended in a courtroom.

timeline.text: The date the story gives (later writers say March 25) for a disc landing in Hart Canyon.
Frank Scully tells the story in his Variety column.
FBI agent Guy Hottel writes a one-page memo on a second-hand report of three saucers recovered in New Mexico.
Behind the Flying Saucers is published and becomes a best-seller.
J. P. Cahn’s article in True magazine exposes the hoax.
Newton and GeBauer are convicted of fraud.
The FBI says the Hottel memo “does not prove the existence of UFOs”.

records.title: Chiles–Whitted encounter
records.place: Near Montgomery, Alabama
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Project Blue Book formally attributed the sighting to a bright meteor (bolide) in 1959.
records.shape: Wingless cigar with two rows of glowing "windows"
records.witnesses: 2 Eastern Air Lines pilots, 1 passenger
records.summary: Eastern Air Lines captain Clarence Chiles and co-pilot John Whitted, flying a DC-3 at about 5,000 ft, saw a glowing torpedo-shaped object rush past their right side and pull up into the clouds. Project Sign took the report so seriously it contributed to the "Estimate of the Situation", which General Vandenberg rejected.

timeline.text: Dull red glow ahead and above; object passes the right wing within seconds.
Object appears to climb into cloud with a burst of flame.
Vandenberg rejects Project Sign’s "Estimate of the Situation".

points.note: Passes the DC-3 on the right

records.title: Gorman dogfight
records.place: Fargo, North Dakota
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The Air Force concluded in 1949 that Gorman had chased a lighted weather balloon.
records.shape: Small blinking ball of light
records.witnesses: P-51 pilot, Piper Cub crew, tower controller
records.summary: North Dakota Air National Guard pilot George Gorman stayed aloft in his P-51 after his flight landed and saw a blinking light that no traffic accounted for. He chased it through turns and steep climbs over Hector Airport until he lost it about 25 miles south-west of Fargo. Tower controllers and a Piper Cub crew also watched the light.

timeline.text: Gorman asks Hector tower about other traffic; none but a Piper Cub.
Head-on passes; object climbs vertically, Gorman stalls at 14,000 ft.
Object last seen heading north-west after Gorman follows it south-west.

points.note: Blinking light west of the stadium

records.title: The green fireballs of New Mexico
records.place: Over northern and central New Mexico, near Los Alamos, Sandia and White Sands
records.explanation: Most scientists then and since take them for bright meteors (bolides), whose green colour comes from metals such as magnesium and nickel burning in the air. Lincoln LaPaz, the University of New Mexico meteor expert who led the first inquiry, argued they were not ordinary meteors: no fragments were ever found, the paths were unusually flat and they seemed to cluster around the nuclear sites. Project Twinkle, the Air Force’s camera watch, ran out without a single useful photograph and concluded they were probably natural.
records.shape: Bright green balls of light, as bright as or brighter than the full Moon, crossing the sky in a flat path and often breaking up
records.witnesses: Airline and military aircrews, security staff at Los Alamos and Sandia, the astronomer Lincoln LaPaz, and later the astrophysicist Donald Menzel
records.duration: Each a few seconds; the reports ran from late 1948 into the early 1950s
records.summary: On the night of December 5, 1948, the crews of two aircraft, one military and one civilian, reported a bright green fireball over New Mexico. Two more pilots reported one on December 8, and on December 12 Lincoln LaPaz saw one himself. He noted that it did not behave like a meteor he knew: it travelled almost level, its path drooped at the end and it broke into fragments that stayed bright green. With the reports clustering around Los Alamos, Sandia and the White Sands range, the Air Force and the Atomic Energy Commission took them seriously. In February 1949 a conference at Los Alamos, with Edward Teller and the geophysicist Joseph Kaplan among those present, could not settle what they were. In December 1949 the Air Force set up Project Twinkle, a network of observation posts and cameras, but it was never fully staffed and was wound up about two years later with no answer beyond “probably natural”.

timeline.text: Two aircrews report a green fireball over New Mexico.
Two more pilots report one.
Lincoln LaPaz sees one and starts an inquiry.
Scientists meet at Los Alamos; no conclusion.
Donald Menzel sees one near Alamogordo and calls it a meteor.
Project Twinkle begins its camera watch.
Twinkle ends without useful photographs; the fireballs are judged probably natural.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Green fireballs

records.title: Arrey, New Mexico — a theodolite track by a Skyhook balloon crew
records.place: About three miles north of Arrey, New Mexico, in the White Sands test area
records.explanation: Blue Book’s record card says “Unidentified”. A pilot balloon released about fifteen minutes later was tracked to show the object could not have been a free balloon at that angular speed. Donald Menzel later proposed a mirage of the crew’s own balloon; Moore rejected it, and the theodolite readings do not fit it well. A meteor does not fit the minute-long track without a trail.
records.shape: A white ellipsoid, about 2.5 times as long as it was wide, light yellow on one side
records.witnesses: Charles B. Moore, a General Mills aerologist, and four Navy enlisted men from White Sands
records.summary: On the clear Sunday morning of April 24, 1949, a General Mills and Navy crew north of Arrey were releasing small pilot balloons to measure the winds before a Skyhook balloon launch. At about 10:20 the aerologist Charles B. Moore looked up from the theodolite, a surveying telescope on a graduated mount, and saw a small white ellipsoid moving fast across the sky. He swung the instrument onto it and, with a stopwatch, the crew followed it for about a minute: it was first at about 45° elevation, moved at roughly five degrees a second, dropped towards 25°, then climbed steeply and was gone. There was no sound, trail or exhaust. The Navy’s Special Devices Center sent Moore’s written report to the Chief of Naval Operations with a letter noting that the readings might indicate controlled flight; Project Grudge and later Blue Book carried the case as unidentified. Ruppelt counted it among the best sightings made at White Sands, and Moore, who later became a respected atmospheric physicist, never accepted the mirage explanation offered for it.

timeline.text: Moore takes over the theodolite and tracks the object; the crew times it with a stopwatch.
After about 60 seconds the object climbs steeply and is lost.
A follow-up pilot balloon is released to compare winds aloft; it is tracked to burst at 93,000 ft.
The Special Devices Center forwards Moore’s statement to the Chief of Naval Operations.
Cdr. R. B. McLaughlin publishes the crew’s data in True magazine.

sources.label: Edward Ruppelt, The Report on Unidentified Flying Objects (1956), Chapter 5 (Project Gutenberg)
The Arrey case: Moore’s report, the record card and the debate (transcribed)

records.title: Clyde Tombaugh’s Las Cruces sighting
records.place: Las Cruces, New Mexico
records.explanation: Tombaugh never said it was a spacecraft. At the time he wrote that he doubted it was a reflection of anything on the ground, as nothing like it had appeared before or since. Later he thought the most likely cause was a reflection from an inversion layer, given how faint the lights were and how they faded as they moved away from the zenith.
records.shape: Six to eight faint, bluish-green rectangles of light in a geometrical group
records.witnesses: Clyde Tombaugh, discoverer of Pluto, his wife and his mother-in-law
records.duration: About 3 seconds (his wife saw it for about 1½ seconds)
records.summary: On the night of August 20, 1949, Clyde Tombaugh, who had found Pluto nineteen years earlier and was then working on missile tracking at White Sands, was sitting in his back yard in Las Cruces with his wife and mother-in-law. He saw a group of six to eight faint, bluish-green rectangles of light, in a fixed arrangement, pass overhead from the north-west and fade as they went toward the south-eastern horizon. “I was so unprepared for such a strange sight that I was really petrified with astonishment,” he wrote. He is probably the most eminent astronomer to have reported a UFO, and he went on to support the scientific study of them, while saying he could not take interstellar visitors seriously.

timeline.text: Tombaugh sees six to eight rectangles of light cross the sky from the zenith toward the south-east.
They fade before reaching the horizon; his wife catches the last 1½ seconds.
He describes the sighting in letters and interviews, ruling out a reflection from the ground.
He writes that an inversion layer is the most likely cause.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Clyde Tombaugh, UFOs

records.title: Farmington “armada” — a town watches discs for three days
records.place: Farmington, New Mexico
records.explanation: The sightings were put down at the time to a Skyhook balloon breaking up, or to drifting cotton-like fluff. James McDonald found that Holloman AFB and the Office of Naval Research, which held the records of every Skyhook release, had none from anywhere in the country on or near that date, that balloon fragments 40,000 to 50,000 ft up would be invisible to the eye, and that the cotton idea came from an offhand remark by a law officer. No Air Force investigation of substance is on record.
records.shape: Discs, mostly silvery, darting in a “bee-like” swarm; one larger and red
records.witnesses: Hundreds of residents over three days, among them the business manager of the Farmington Daily Times and a former Navy pilot
records.duration: Mostly late morning, on three consecutive days
records.summary: For three days in the middle of March 1950, people in Farmington, in the far north-west of New Mexico, reported flying saucers over the town, and the largest sighting, on the late morning of Friday, March 17, was watched by hundreds. The Farmington Daily Times’ front page the next day had estimates from several to more than 500 objects; one witness who tried to triangulate one put its speed at about 1,000 mph. When the physicist James McDonald interviewed seven witnesses eighteen years later, the Times business manager Clayton Boddy estimated he had seen 20 to 30 discs, including one much larger red one, and the realtor John Eaton, a former Navy pilot, put them at around 15,000 ft, darting about “like bees” and turning from flat to round as they tilted. No one reported wings or tails. McDonald checked the explanation then current, a Skyhook balloon breaking up, and found no Skyhook had been released; he told a House committee in 1968 that he saw “no ready explanation”. The case remains a mass sighting with no instrument record.

timeline.text: First reports of discs over Farmington.
The largest sighting: hundreds of residents watch dozens of objects.
The Farmington Daily Times runs the story on its front page.
McDonald presents the case to the House Committee on Science and Astronautics.

sources.label: Farmington Daily Times, March 18, 1950 (transcribed)

records.title: McMinnville (Trent) photographs
records.place: Trent farm near Sheridan / McMinnville, Oregon
records.explanation: The Condon Committee called it one of the few cases where the evidence was consistent with the witnesses’ account; skeptics (Sheaffer, Maccabee critics, later photogrammetry) argue it was a small model hung from overhead wires.
records.shape: Metallic disc with a raised "mast"
records.witnesses: Paul and Evelyn Trent
records.summary: Evelyn Trent saw a metallic disc moving slowly over the farm; her husband Paul took two photographs with a box camera. The images ran in LIFE magazine and became among the most analysed UFO photos ever taken.

timeline.text: Disc seen over the farmyard; two photographs taken.
Published in the McMinnville Telephone-Register, then LIFE.
Condon Report Case 46 analysis.

points.note: Seen to the north-east, drifting west

records.title: Farnborough test pilot’s disc — the Flying Saucer Working Party
records.place: Royal Aircraft Establishment, Farnborough, Hampshire
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The Ministry of Defence’s Flying Saucer Working Party (report DSI/JTIC No. 7, June 1951) judged the first sighting an optical illusion, and the second, by six officers, a normal aircraft manoeuvring at extreme visual range, seen by men already influenced by the first report. It recommended that no further investigation of “mystery aerial phenomena” be undertaken.
records.shape: A flat, light pearl-grey disc “like a shirt button”
records.witnesses: Flt Lt Stanley Hubbard, an RAF test pilot; about two weeks later, he and five other senior officers
records.summary: One morning in August 1950 Flight Lieutenant Stanley Hubbard, an experienced RAF test pilot at the Royal Aircraft Establishment, saw a flat, pearl-grey disc spinning through S-turns over the airfield at what he judged to be up to 1,000 mph. About two weeks later he and five other senior officers watched a disc low in the sky towards Guildford and Farnham perform high-speed manoeuvres and a “falling leaf” motion before diving towards the horizon. The reports reached Sir Henry Tizard, the Ministry of Defence’s chief scientific adviser, who in October 1950 set up a small “Flying Saucer” Working Party to study such reports. All six officers were interviewed. The working party’s report of June 1951 explained the Farnborough sightings, and every other report it studied, as misidentified aircraft, balloons and astronomical objects, optical illusions or hoaxes. It stayed secret until it was released to the researchers David Clarke and Andy Roberts in 2001; the file is DEFE 44/119 at The National Archives.

timeline.text: Hubbard sees a pearl-grey disc over the RAE airfield.
He and five officers see a disc towards Guildford and Farnham.
Sir Henry Tizard sets up the Flying Saucer Working Party.
Report DSI/JTIC No. 7: optical illusion and an aircraft at extreme range.
The report is released to researchers.

sources.label: The National Archives — DEFE 44/119, Unidentified Flying Objects (DSI/JTIC Report No. 7), 1951
David Clarke — The Flying Saucer Working Party
Wikipedia — Flying Saucer Working Party

records.title: Mariana film, Great Falls
records.place: Great Falls, Montana
records.explanation: The Air Force suggested reflections from two F-94 jets landing nearby; later analyses dispute the geometry.
records.shape: Two bright spinning discs
records.witnesses: Nicholas Mariana and his secretary
records.summary: Great Falls Electrics baseball manager Nicholas Mariana filmed two bright objects crossing the sky with his 16 mm camera. The Air Force returned the film with frames missing; the case was studied by Project Blue Book, the Robertson Panel and the Condon Committee.

timeline.text: Two bright objects filmed moving south-east over the city.
Shown to the CIA-sponsored Robertson Panel.

records.title: U.S. Navy R5D — object over the North Atlantic
records.place: North Atlantic, east of Newfoundland
records.explanation: The Blue Book record card gives its consulting astronomer's view that the crew saw an astronomical display. The crew said it was a solid object that came up to meet them.
records.shape: Huge yellowish glow, semicircular
records.witnesses: Navy flight crew and passengers
records.summary: A U.S. Navy R5D transport flying toward Newfoundland at about 10,000 ft saw a yellowish glow, like a fire, ahead and below. It rushed toward the aircraft and grew very large and bright, with a semicircular shape. Then it turned 180° and vanished over the horizon at great speed. The Air Force logged the report at 49°50′N 50°03′W. Crew member Lt. Graham Bethune later described it publicly.

timeline.text: Glow seen ahead of the aircraft, low over the sea.
It closes rapidly and fills the view, bright and semicircular.
It turns 180° and leaves at "terrific speed".
Crew report forwarded to Air Force intelligence.

points.note: Position in the Blue Book record

records.title: Lubbock Lights
records.place: Lubbock, Texas
records.explanation: Project Blue Book’s Edward Ruppelt concluded the lights were probably plovers reflecting street lights; the photos themselves were never shown to be faked.
records.shape: V / arc formation of 15–30 bluish lights
records.witnesses: Texas Tech professors, residents
records.duration: Seconds per pass; repeated over weeks
records.summary: Starting on 25 August 1951, three Texas Tech professors saw arcs of faint lights sweep silently overhead several times. On 30–31 August, 18-year-old Carl Hart Jr. photographed a V-shaped formation of lights from his backyard.

timeline.text: Professors see the first passes of the formation.
Carl Hart Jr. photographs the lights.
Ruppelt investigates for Project Blue Book.

records.title: Fort Monmouth radar and T-33 sighting
records.place: Fort Monmouth and the Jersey Shore, New Jersey
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Blue Book's record card: "Extensive investigation revealed that the target on 10 Sept was caused by a balloon. Targets on 11 September were attributed to anomalous propagation."
records.shape: Fast radar target; silver disc seen from a T-33
records.witnesses: Army radar operators; two Air Force pilots
records.summary: During a demonstration at the Army Signal Corps radar school at Fort Monmouth, an operator picked up a low target moving too fast for the automatic tracking. Minutes later, the crew of an Air Force T-33 over Point Pleasant reported a silver disc below them and dived after it. More radar targets followed the next day. The case alarmed the Pentagon and led the Air Force to reorganise Project Grudge, which became Project Blue Book.

timeline.text: SCR-584 radar at Fort Monmouth picks up a fast target it cannot lock on to.
T-33 crew over Point Pleasant see a silver disc below and give chase.
Further radar targets reported by the Signal Corps.
Investigation; Project Grudge is reorganised under Capt. Edward Ruppelt.

points.note: Passes the radar faster than it can track
Disc seen below, over Point Pleasant
Dives after it; object pulls away out to sea

records.title: Long Beach — six F-86s chase an object they cannot reach
records.place: Over Long Beach, California
records.explanation: Blue Book’s record card evaluates it as a balloon: a radiosonde released from Long Beach Municipal Airport was near the fighters’ path, and the first pair were looking almost straight at it when they first saw the object. Ruppelt, who plotted the balloon (tracked by radio fixes) against the F-86s (tracked by radar), wrote that the paths agreed only at that first moment, that the weather observers watching their balloon saw no fighters near it, and that it burst about ten minutes before the pilots lost sight of the object.
records.shape: A silver aircraft with sharply swept wings, or round and silver; orbiting slowly to the left
records.witnesses: Seven Air Force F-86 pilots and their ground controller
records.summary: At 7:55 a.m. on September 23, 1951, two F-86 Sabres on an early patrol, approaching Long Beach on the west leg of the radio range, saw an object high ahead, in a slow left-hand turn. The ground radar had nothing, and the controller sent them up after it, but they could not climb to it; whenever they seemed to gain, it rose a little and stayed out of reach, still circling. Running short of fuel after about ten minutes, they were relieved by four more F-86s scrambled from George AFB, which worked in pairs for another half hour to reach what they put at 50,000 to 55,000 ft, then also turned back; a seventh fighter arrived to find nothing. All but one pilot described a silver aircraft with highly swept-back wings; one said it looked round. Edwards AFB, Nellis, Inyokern and George had nothing in the air that could fly that high. Blue Book later put it down to a weather balloon; Ruppelt, who tried to make that answer fit, could not.

timeline.text: Two F-86s on the west leg of the Long Beach range see an object high ahead, orbiting left.
Low on fuel, they are relieved by four F-86s scrambled from George AFB.
The relief flight gives up below the object; a seventh F-86 arrives to find it gone.
Intelligence and OSI reports; the pilots are re-interrogated and balloon data is gathered.
Blue Book evaluates it as a radiosonde balloon; Ruppelt doubts it.

sources.label: Project Blue Book file, Long Beach, September 1951 (Internet Archive)
Edward Ruppelt, The Report on Unidentified Flying Objects (1956), Chapters 7–9 (Project Gutenberg)

records.title: Mitchel AFB — a Navy TBM chases a “parachute” over Long Island
records.place: Mitchel Air Force Base, Hempstead, Long Island, New York
records.explanation: The base weather section launched a Rawinsonde balloon at 09:50 from south-east of the field, and Blue Book’s analysts believed the pilot saw it. Ruppelt, who interviewed him, noted that the balloon drifted south-east and never passed north of the field, where the pilot followed the object, and that it pulled away from him in a straight chase, which a balloon cannot do.
records.shape: Dome-shaped like a parachute canopy, white with a dark underside; rocking as it flew
records.witnesses: A Navy pilot from the Special Devices Center at Port Washington, flying a TBM-3W
records.duration: About two and a half minutes
records.summary: At about 9:50 a.m. on January 21, 1952, a Navy pilot who had just taken off from Mitchel AFB in a TBM Avenger saw below him, south-east of the field, what he took for the canopy of a parachute. Realising it was moving across the wind, he climbed after it as it climbed, tried to cut inside its left turn, overshot and passed over it, then dived to get behind it. It turned through 180 degrees, swung round the north side of the base gaining speed, and outran him; he last saw it crossing the coast near Freeport, heading out to sea. He put it at 200 to 300 ft over houses at first and its speed at several hundred knots by the end. The tower did not see it. Ruppelt went to New York to interview him and thought him careful and reliable; he wrote that unless the pilot was several miles from where he believed, the object could not have been the weather balloon released that morning.

timeline.text: The TBM, just airborne, sees a white “parachute” south-east of the field; the weather section releases a balloon.
The pilot climbs after it, overshoots, then pulls in behind it.
It turns, swings round the north edge of the base and accelerates away.
Last seen crossing the coast near Freeport, heading out to sea.
Ruppelt interviews the pilot; Blue Book believes the balloon was the answer.

Project Blue Book file with the balloon analysis (Internet Archive)

records.title: Wonsan and Sunchon B-29 sightings
records.place: Wonsan and Sunchon, North Korea
records.explanation: No explanation was ever settled. Air Force Lt. Gen. Otto Weyland said that “we can’t say there’s nothing to it” but that without more data a conclusive answer could not be expected, and he doubted that jet aircraft were responsible.
records.shape: Orange sphere or disc, with occasional blue flames
records.witnesses: Two B-29 crews from different squadrons
records.duration: Five minutes or more at Wonsan; about a minute at Sunchon
records.summary: Around midnight on the night of January 29, 1952, during the Korean War, the rear gunner and the central fire-control gunner of a B-29 Superfortress at 20,000 feet over Wonsan saw an orange, globe-shaped light about three feet across that stayed near the bomber for five minutes or more. A second B-29 from a different squadron, hundreds of miles away at Sunchon, reported a lighted orange sphere that followed it for about a minute on the way back to base. The two reports were made independently by trained aircrew over hostile territory, and the story was widely published in February 1952. Air Force UFO experts have argued that the wide publicity it received helped feed the 1952 wave, which ended over Washington, D.C.

timeline.text: The gunners of the first B-29 see an orange light near the aircraft at 20,000 ft over Wonsan.
The light stays with the bomber for five minutes or more at about 200 mph.
A second B-29 returning to base at Sunchon reports an orange sphere following it for about a minute.
The reports are published; Lt. Gen. Weyland says more data would be needed for an answer.

records.title: Barra da Tijuca — the O Cruzeiro disc photographs
records.place: Coast at Barra da Tijuca, near Pedra do Marisco, Rio de Janeiro
records.explanation: Donald Menzel and Lyle Boyd called the photographs a hoax because the disc is lit from the left while the hillside and trees below it are lit from the right; the Condon study’s own enlargement supported that objection. Brazilian Air Force analysts had said a hoax was impossible, but no independent study of the negatives was ever made and neither man admitted a fake.
records.shape: A flat disc with a raised rim, seen sideways and tilted
records.witnesses: Two O Cruzeiro staff: photographer Ed Keffel and reporter João Martins
records.summary: On the afternoon of May 7, 1952, the reporter João Martins and the photographer Ed Keffel of the weekly magazine O Cruzeiro were on the coast at Barra da Tijuca, south of Rio, when Martins pointed out what he first took for an aircraft “flying sideways”. Keffel took five photographs with a Rolleiflex in about a minute, and the magazine published them as a flying disc. They became famous across South America, and Brazilian Air Force officers reportedly declared a hoax impossible after studying the distances. In 1963 Menzel and Boyd pointed out that the disc is lit from the opposite side to the palm and the hillside beneath it, which a single sunlit scene cannot do. William Hartmann made an independent enlargement for the Condon study (1968), found that it supported the objection, and noted that the case was offered as incontrovertible while containing “a simple, internal inconsistency”. The study never interviewed the photographers, and the case has no other witnesses.

timeline.text: Martins and Keffel see the object over the coast; Keffel takes five photographs in about a minute.
O Cruzeiro publishes the pictures as a flying disc.
Menzel and Boyd point out that the disc and the landscape are lit from opposite sides.
The Condon study’s enlargement supports the objection (case 48).

Wikipedia — UFO sightings in Brazil (1952)

records.title: Tremonton, Utah film
records.place: Near Tremonton, Utah
records.explanation: Navy photo analysts could not identify the objects; the 1953 Robertson Panel suggested seagulls reflecting sunlight. The film was re-released in 2026 as PURSUE record DOW-UAP-PR159.
records.shape: About a dozen bright objects milling in the sky
records.witnesses: Navy Chief Warrant Officer Delbert C. Newhouse and family
records.summary: Driving about seven miles north of Tremonton, Navy photographer Delbert Newhouse stopped and filmed a group of bright objects with his Bell & Howell 16 mm camera. The Navy’s Photographic Interpretation Laboratory spent over 1,000 man-hours on it and ruled out aircraft and birds; the Robertson Panel disagreed.

timeline.text: Newhouse stops the car and films the objects moving west.
Navy lab analysis: not aircraft or birds.
Robertson Panel suggests seagulls.
Digitised film published in PURSUE Release 06.

records.title: Nash–Fortenberry sighting
records.place: Chesapeake Bay near Newport News, Virginia
records.explanation: Listed as "unknown" by Project Blue Book. Menzel suggested haze-distorted ground lights or fireflies; others a mirage of Venus.
records.shape: Eight glowing red-orange discs in echelon
records.witnesses: 2 Pan Am pilots; independent ground witnesses

records.title: Salem Coast Guard Air Station photograph
records.place: U.S. Coast Guard Air Station Salem, Winter Island, Salem, Massachusetts
records.explanation: Blue Book’s analysts went back and forth: a probable double exposure, then probably reflections of lights on the window glass, and in the end the case was filed as unexplained. Against the reflection idea, the parked cars in the photograph reflect the sun but not the lights, and some accounts say the window was open, with only a screen.
records.shape: Four elliptical blobs of light in formation, with rays
records.witnesses: Shell Alpert, a Coast Guard photographer’s mate; a second Coastguardsman reportedly saw the lights
records.summary: At 9:35 a.m. on July 16, 1952, Shell Alpert, a photographer at the Coast Guard Air Station in Salem, Massachusetts, saw bright lights through the window of the station’s photo laboratory and took a single picture: four elliptical blobs of light, apparently in formation, above the parked cars. It was taken in the middle of that summer’s wave of sightings and was soon in the newspapers. Blue Book’s file, case 1501, holds sixteen photographs and a series of analyses: the first suggested a double exposure, a second that the “objects” were reflections of interior lights on the glass, a test with a photo-flood lamp showed that a real light source would also have been reflected in the cars, which these are not, and the case finished as unexplained. It is one of the best-known UFO photographs, and one of the plainest examples of how hard a single frame is to settle.

timeline.text: Alpert photographs four lights through the photo-lab window.
Blue Book case 1501: double exposure, then reflections, then unexplained.

records.title: Carson Sink — two colonels in a B-25 meet three deltas
records.place: Over the Carson Sink, Nevada, on the airway to Salt Lake City
records.explanation: Blue Book checked Flight Service records (no aircraft near), the Navy and Air Force delta-wing aircraft (none there; the Air Force’s only delta was grounded) and every weather and research balloon flight (none), and carried the case as unknown. Ruppelt’s own speculations, F-86s flying where they should not, missing records or a misjudged distance, were offered only as possibilities.
records.shape: Three bright silver delta-wing craft with no tails or canopies, a ridge from nose to tail
records.witnesses: Two Air Force colonels, both command pilots stationed at the Pentagon
records.summary: On July 24, 1952, two Air Force colonels flying a B-25 from Hamilton AFB to Colorado Springs crossed the Sierra Nevada and were heading east at 11,000 ft on the airway “Green 3” towards Salt Lake City. At 3:40 p.m., over the Carson Sink, one of them saw three objects ahead and to the right that looked like F-86s in a tight V. Within seconds they were close enough to see clearly: bright silver deltas with no tails and no canopies, only a ridge running from nose to tail. The three made a slight left bank and passed the bomber within 400 to 800 yards at what the pilots put at three times the speed of an F-86. Both were command pilots with thousands of hours, whose work would have shown them anything the United States had flying; both had been sceptics. They reported it on landing, and Blue Book’s checks found no aircraft, no delta and no balloon to account for it. Ruppelt used it in his book as an example of a report that ends simply “Unknown”.

timeline.text: The B-25 leaves Hamilton AFB for Colorado Springs.
Over the Carson Sink at 11,000 ft, three deltas pass within 400 to 800 yards.
The colonels report the sighting to Air Defense Command at Colorado Springs.
Blue Book checks aircraft, deltas and balloons, and finds nothing.

records.title: The Florida scoutmaster — burned, and called a hoax
records.place: Palmetto scrub off a back road inland from West Palm Beach, Florida
records.explanation: Blue Book wrote it off as a hoax, mainly because of the scoutmaster’s record and reputation, the press agent he hired and a re-enactment showing the scouts could not have seen him fall where they said. Ruppelt, who led the investigation, admitted they could not prove a hoax and that the two pieces of physical evidence, tiny burned holes in his cap and grass roots charred as if the ground had been heated to about 300 °F from below, were never explained.
records.shape: A dark, round, slightly concave craft about 30 ft overhead, with a dome and vanes around the rim; a ball of red fire
records.witnesses: D. S. “Sonny” Desvergers, a scoutmaster, and three Boy Scouts in his car; a deputy sheriff and a constable afterwards
records.summary: On the evening of August 19, 1952, Sonny Desvergers, a scoutmaster in his early thirties, was driving three scouts home along a black-top road through palmetto scrub inland from West Palm Beach when he saw lights in the pines and stopped. He told the boys to fetch help if he was not back in fifteen minutes and went into the scrub with a machete and two flashlights. By his account he came into a clearing, felt heat, and saw a dark disc about 30 ft above him; when he shone his light on it, a small ball of red fire drifted down, became a mist, and he blacked out. The scouts said they saw a red ball engulf him and ran to a farmhouse; a deputy and a constable found him coming out of the brush, badly frightened, with his forearms, face and cap lightly burned. Ruppelt flew down from Dayton the next day. The burns were like mild sunburn, which a flight surgeon could reproduce with a cigarette lighter. Blue Book found the scoutmaster’s record did not match the story he told of himself, concluded it was a hoax, and called it “the best hoax in UFO history”; but a laboratory found the roots of the grass under where the object was said to hover charred and the blades unharmed, which nobody could explain.

timeline.text: Desvergers stops to look at lights in the scrub and walks in; the scouts see a red ball of fire.
The scouts fetch help; a deputy and a constable find him at the roadside with light burns.
Ruppelt and a Blue Book team fly to Florida; a flight surgeon examines him.
Laboratories test the machete, the cap and soil and grass samples; a second trip re-enacts the scene.
Blue Book files the case as a hoax; the charred roots stay unexplained.

records.title: Ellsworth AFB — the Black Hawk light and the F-84 chase
records.place: Black Hawk and Ellsworth Air Force Base, Rapid City, South Dakota; later Bismarck, North Dakota
records.explanation: Project Blue Book carried the case as unsolved. The Condon study (1968) attributed the Rapid City and Bismarck sightings to stars seen through a temperature inversion, at least one meteor, anomalous-propagation and ghost echoes on the ground radar, and a faulty radar gunsight in the F-84; the Blue Book investigator had suggested Capella low in the north, a balloon or a meteor.
records.shape: A bright light, white turning green; red-to-white lights later
records.witnesses: A Ground Observer Corps volunteer, radar controllers, airmen and two F-84 pilots
records.duration: About 20:05 to 02:50 MST, on and off
records.summary: At about 8:05 p.m. on August 5, 1953, a Ground Observer Corps volunteer at Black Hawk, west of Rapid City, reported a bright light to the Air Defense Command radar station at Ellsworth AFB. The controller saw blips through the ground clutter, and airmen sent outside watched a light cross from north to south. F-84 fighters on patrol were vectored onto the returns. One pilot saw only a brief, very bright light; the second climbed from 15,000 to 26,000 ft after a white light that turned green and was “considerably brighter than a star”, said it “definitely moved in relation to the stars”, and chased it for about 80 miles to the north while the controller tracked both on radar. His radar gunsight’s warning light came on, but the gun camera produced nothing usable. After midnight the Bismarck filter center, told to look for flying saucers, reported more lights. Capt. Edward Ruppelt flew to Rapid City to investigate himself; Blue Book filed the case as unsolved, and the Condon study later explained it as stars, a meteor and radar artefacts.

timeline.text: The Black Hawk observer reports a bright light; the Ellsworth radar controller comes on duty.
Blips are seen through ground clutter; airmen outside see a light moving north to south.

records.title: The Nowra Sea Fury — two lights on the radar
records.place: South-west of Goulburn, New South Wales, on the way back to Naval Air Station Nowra
records.explanation: The Navy found no explanation. A minute paper at the Fleet Air Arm Museum records that no RAAF aircraft were nearby and that the only other aircraft in the area was a TAA Convair airliner, which does not account for two lights that crossed in front of the fighter and were painted beside it on radar. The Directorate of Naval Intelligence called the pilot “an entirely credible witness”.
records.shape: Two very bright white lights, each on top of a large, vague dark mass
records.witnesses: Lt J. A. “Shamus” O’Farrell, RAN, the Sea Fury pilot; PO Keith Jessop on the Nowra radar; a ground witness
records.summary: On the evening of August 31, 1954, Lieutenant James O’Farrell of 723 Squadron was flying a Hawker Sea Fury home to Nowra at 220 knots after a night cross-country flight through Young, Temora and Yass. At about 7:10 p.m., south-west of Goulburn, he called Nowra and then saw a very bright light closing fast from one o’clock; it crossed ahead of him and took up station on his left, seeming to orbit. A second, similar light appeared at nine o’clock, passed about a mile in front and joined it. Close up he could make out only “a vague shape with the white light situated centrally on top”, a large dark mass with no other lights. He asked Nowra about other traffic; the radar operator, Petty Officer Keith Jessop, had two returns in company with the Sea Fury, and O’Farrell turned through 180 and then 360 degrees so that radar could pick out which return was his. The two lights re-formed and left to the north-east at great speed, and radar followed them for a while. O’Farrell landed at about 7:30 p.m., was examined by a surgeon commander and wrote a report that the Navy kept classified until 1982. J. Allen Hynek interviewed him in 1973.

records.title: Quarouble railway encounter — Marius Dewilde
records.place: Quarouble, near Valenciennes, Nord, France
records.explanation: The marks on the sleepers were real, and an investigator thought they could be landing struts. But there was one witness, who had suffered a head injury the year before and later had nervous disorders, and the air police and gendarmes found no footprints or other proof.

records.witnesses: Marius Dewilde, a 34-year-old metalworker
records.summary: On the night of September 10, 1954, Marius Dewilde, living beside a level crossing on the Saint-Amand–Blanc-Misseron line, went into his yard after his dog barked. He saw a dark mass on the tracks and two small figures, about a metre tall with large heads like glass helmets, heading for it. When he approached, a bright light left him unable to move; the object rose and vanished to the west. Air police inspectors found symmetrical dents in the wooden sleepers at five places and displaced ballast, and one of them said the marks might fit landing struts. It became one of the best-known cases of the 1954 wave of sightings in France.

records.title: Gravataí Air Base — the Brazilian Air Force communiqué
records.place: Gravataí Air Base (today Canoas Air Force Base), near Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul
records.shape: Circular objects of a dull silvery colour, moving erratically
records.witnesses: Air Force officers, sergeants and soldiers at the base, and civilians
records.summary: Between about 1 and 3 p.m. on October 24, 1954, officers, sergeants and soldiers at the Brazilian Air Force base then called Gravataí, near Porto Alegre, watched circular, dull-silver objects over the base. Two days later the base command issued a communiqué: the objects’ speed and height could not be measured but were far beyond those of anything known, their course was erratic and they returned to earlier positions, they could not be confused with known celestial bodies, and no weather balloons were in the area. The base reported to the Air Force general command, asked for an investigation and invited civilians to send in their own reports, while its commander forbade staff to talk to the press until experts had studied the evidence. On November 16, 1954, Brigadier Gervásio Duncan released summaries of five of sixteen reports selected by the Air Force, two of them about Gravataí, and declined to speculate on what the objects were beyond saying that the observers were well qualified. No explanation was published; the communiqué survives through contemporary press reports collected by the Brazilian researcher Olavo Fontes.

timeline.text: Base personnel begin watching circular silvery objects over Gravataí.

records.place: Mitchell Flat, east of Marfa, Texas
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Observers from the University of Texas at Dallas (2004) and a study over 2000–2008 concluded that most lights are car headlights on U.S. 67, distorted by layers of warm and cool desert air, along with ranch lights and campfires.
records.shape: Glowing orbs that split, merge and drift
records.witnesses: Visitors to the viewing area, nightly
records.summary: Lights seen on the desert toward the Chinati Mountains, south-west of the Marfa Lights Viewing Area on U.S. 90, are said to bob, split, merge and change colour. Local lore traces them to a cowhand in 1883, but the first published account is a 1957 Coronet magazine article. The town now promotes them to tourists.

timeline.text: Cowhand Robert Reed Ellison's account (published much later).
First magazine article, in Coronet.
UT Dallas students match lights to headlights on U.S. 67.

records.title: RB-47 radar–ECM–visual encounter
records.place: Gulf Coast to Oklahoma
records.explanation: Condon Report Case 5 concluded the crew’s recollections were "not adequate to allow identification"; skeptics have proposed a mix of airliner lights and ground radar. Physicist James McDonald considered it among the strongest cases.
records.shape: Intense white / red light; 2.8–3 GHz radar-like signal
records.witnesses: 6-man USAF RB-47H crew; ground radar operators
records.summary: An RB-47H electronic-reconnaissance jet of the 55th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing was paced across Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas by a source seen visually by the pilots, detected by the ECM operators’ direction-finding gear, and painted by ground radar at the same position. The source blinked off on all three channels at once, then reappeared.

Pilots see a white light cross in front of them near Winnsboro, Louisiana.
"Huge light" seen near Dallas, 5,000 ft below; 34,500 ft altitude.
Duncanville ADC radar ("Utah") confirms a target at the ECM bearing.
Object stops and blinks out on radar, ECM and visual simultaneously.
Signal finally fades near Oklahoma City.
