records.title: Portuguese Air Force F-84s — the Lemos Ferreira sighting
records.place: Over the Portuguese–Spanish border region, returning to Ota air base
records.shape: A yellowish sphere that swelled and shrank, turned red and “sausage-shaped”, and released four smaller yellow spheres
records.witnesses: Capt. José Lemos Ferreira and the pilots of three other F-84G Thunderjets
records.summary: On the night of September 4, 1957, four Portuguese Air Force F-84G Thunderjets from Ota were on a night navigation exercise into Spain, led by Capt. José Lemos Ferreira, who later became Chief of Staff of the Air Force (1977–1984). At about 9,000 m the pilots saw a yellowish sphere just above the horizon that “was not a star, a planet or a comet”; it grew and shrank, “in seconds, turning from a billiard ball into a basketball”, became intense red and elongated, and four smaller yellow spheres separated from it and took up positions around it. When one pilot felt the objects were closing on them fast, the formation broke up; when it re-formed, nothing was visible. The pilots wrote a joint report, which Ferreira believed was passed to NATO; it has not been published. Accounts disagree on the route (towards Córdoba and Cáceres, or back from Granada over Portalegre and Coruche). Ferreira, who never offered an explanation, noted that hunters near Coruche saw “a dance of lights” at the same time, and that the Coimbra geophysical institute recorded magnetic disturbances.

timeline.text: Four F-84Gs leave Ota on a night navigation flight towards Spain.
A yellowish sphere is seen above the horizon; it changes size and colour.
Four small spheres separate from it; the formation breaks to avoid them.
Nothing is visible when the formation re-forms.
Ferreira, by then a retired general, recounts the sighting to the Lusa news agency.

records.title: Ubatuba magnesium fragments
records.place: Ubatuba, São Paulo, Brazil
records.explanation: The fragments are real and were analysed, but the story of their origin rests on a letter from an unnamed reader. Later isotope analyses found ordinary terrestrial magnesium, and sceptics regard the tale as a hoax.
records.shape: Disc that exploded over the sea (as told)
records.witnesses: A fisherman and friends (reported in a letter)
records.summary: On September 14, 1957 the Rio de Janeiro columnist Ibrahim Sued printed a letter, with three small pieces of white metal, from a reader who said he had watched a disc explode over the sea near Ubatuba and had picked up fragments. A laboratory of Brazil’s Ministry of Agriculture and a second spectrographic analysis found the metal to be extremely pure magnesium. Ufologists, among them James Harder, argued that purity that high was hard to make at the time; later analyses of the isotopes gave normal Earth ratios, and the origin of the pieces remains unproven.

timeline.text: A reader writes to the columnist, describing a disc exploding over the sea off Ubatuba.
The column prints the letter, with three small pieces of white metal.
Brazilian laboratories find almost pure magnesium; later tests find ordinary isotopes.

sources.label: UFO Evidence — The Ubatuba, Brazil fragments

records.title: Antônio Vilas-Boas abduction claim
records.place: São Francisco de Sales, Minas Gerais, Brazil
records.explanation: It is one account by one man, first told months afterwards. The researcher Peter Rogerson doubts it, noting that a similar story ran in the magazine O Cruzeiro in November 1957, before Vilas-Boas first reported his, and arguing that he may have borrowed details from it and from the contactee George Adamski.
records.shape: Circular or egg-shaped craft with a rotating cupola
records.witnesses: Antônio Vilas-Boas, a 23-year-old farmer (the only witness)
records.summary: Antônio Vilas-Boas, a farmer working at night in a field, said that on the night of October 15–16, 1957 a circular craft landed near him and that five-foot beings in grey coveralls seized him, took him aboard, took blood from his chin and exposed him to an unknown gas. He also described a sexual encounter with a female being, and said the whole episode lasted about four hours. In February 1958 Dr. Olavo Fontes of Brazil’s National School of Medicine examined him and concluded he had been exposed to a large dose of radiation, with mild radiation sickness: pains, nausea, headaches, loss of appetite and skin lesions that appeared over the following months. It is often cited as one of the earliest well-known abduction stories, and it is widely doubted.

timeline.text: Vilas-Boas says a craft lands near his field and that he is taken aboard for about four hours.
He reports pains, nausea, headaches, loss of appetite and skin lesions.
A similar story appears in O Cruzeiro, before he first reports his own.
Dr. Olavo Fontes examines him and finds signs of mild radiation sickness.

records.title: Levelland vehicle-stopping reports
records.place: Levelland, Texas
records.explanation: Project Blue Book attributed the reports to ball lightning / an electrical storm; weather records showed drizzle but little lightning.
records.shape: Glowing egg-shaped object, 100–200 ft
records.witnesses: 15+ motorists, sheriff, fire chief
records.summary: Over roughly three hours, motorists on several highways around Levelland independently reported a glowing, egg-shaped object on or over the road; each said their engine and headlights died until it left. Sheriff Weir Clem and Fire Chief Ray Jones saw lights as well.

timeline.text: Pedro Saucedo reports a blue flash and a rocket-shaped object 4 mi west of town.

records.title: White Sands military police patrols
records.place: White Sands Proving Ground (up-range), New Mexico
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Project Blue Book concluded the first patrol saw the half-full Moon through broken cloud, with the drifting cloud creating the apparent motion, and the second saw Venus, then near its greatest brilliance.
records.shape: Reddish-orange, egg-shaped light
records.witnesses: Two U.S. Army military police patrols
records.summary: Hours after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, and on the same night as the Levelland sightings in Texas, two Army MP patrols in jeeps reported lights up-range. At about 2:30 a.m. the first saw a brilliant, reddish-orange egg-shaped light hover for about three minutes, then descend and disappear. That evening a second patrol saw a glowing object that climbed until it looked like a star. The reports reached the newspapers during the November 1957 wave. Air Force investigators found the young soldiers had talked over their sightings before reporting them.

timeline.text: First patrol sees an egg-shaped light hover for ~3 minutes, then descend.

records.title: Fort Itaipu sentries burned
records.place: Fort Itaipu, Praia Grande, São Paulo
records.shape: Bright orange light descending from the sky
records.witnesses: 2 sentries; garrison woken by the power failure
records.summary: In the early hours, the day after Sputnik 2, two sentries at the coastal Fort Itaipu saw a bright orange light descend and stop above the fort. They said a wave of intense heat followed and both collapsed with burns. The fort's electricity failed, including the emergency circuits. Brazilian military investigators interviewed the soldiers, and American officials were reported to have joined them.

records.title: Kirtland Air Force Base tower sighting
records.place: Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Capt. Shere of Ent AFB, who interviewed the controllers for Project Blue Book, found nothing a small private aircraft could not do and concluded that was what they saw; the radar returns matched a small plane. The Condon Report agreed, suggesting a pilot who had strayed onto the military field by mistake. The physicist James McDonald, who later spoke to the controllers, said they found the explanation amusing.
records.shape: Egg-shaped object, 15–20 ft tall, with a single white light at its base
records.witnesses: CAA tower controllers R. M. Kaser and E. G. Brink
records.duration: About a minute in view; about 20 minutes on radar
records.summary: At about 10:45 p.m. on November 4, 1957, in the week of the Levelland sightings, two Civil Aeronautics Administration controllers in the tower at Kirtland AFB saw a white light cross the airfield eastward. A dark object then came down steeply near the end of runway 26 and crossed the field a few tens of feet up. Through binoculars it looked egg-shaped, 15 to 20 feet tall, with one white light at its base. It hovered within 3,000 feet of the tower for up to a minute, moved east to the base boundary and climbed fast into the overcast. Albuquerque Radar Approach Control tracked a target that turned south, circled near the low-frequency range station, hovered over the outer marker, then followed a departing C-46 for about 14 miles before returning to the marker and fading. Radar contact lasted about 20 minutes.

It crosses the field a few tens of feet up and hovers within 3,000 ft of the tower.
It moves to the east boundary and climbs fast into the overcast.
Approach Control radar has it moving east, then south, circling near the range station.
It hovers over the outer marker and follows a departing C-46 for about 14 miles.
Back over the outer marker, the return fades.

records.title: Coast Guard cutter Sebago — radar contacts in the Gulf of Mexico
records.place: USCGC Sebago, about 200 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi, Gulf of Mexico
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Blue Book evaluated the radar contacts as false targets from anomalous propagation and the visual sighting as a meteor. The Condon study’s radar analyst agreed that the visual object was a meteor and the echoes most likely anomalous propagation, with the first target possibly an aircraft. The news reports of a single craft circling the ship were built from separate, unrelated contacts.
records.shape: Radar targets; one brilliant light “like a planet” crossing for three seconds
records.witnesses: The cutter’s radar operators and four men on deck
records.duration: 27 minutes on radar; the light three seconds
records.summary: At 5:10 a.m. on November 5, 1957, during the wave of sightings that followed Levelland and the launch of Sputnik 2, the Coast Guard cutter Sebago was steaming north about 200 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi when its radar picked up a target 14 miles off, moving north to south. Over the next 27 minutes the log records a string of contacts: one closing to two miles and passing up the port side, then lost, others at 22 and 55 miles, one stationary at seven miles, and the last at 175 miles. At 5:21 four men on deck saw a brilliant light, like a planet, cross part of the sky to the north-west for three seconds. The navigator’s estimates of the target’s speed, from 1,000 to 3,300 mph, made the papers, which described one object circling the ship. Blue Book and later the Condon study treated the light as a meteor and the radar targets as unrelated echoes.

timeline.text: First radar contact, bearing 290°, 14 miles, moving north to south.
A target closes to two miles and passes along the port side; lost at 05:14.
Contacts at 22 and 55 miles, then one stationary at 7 miles.
A brilliant light is seen for three seconds, from 270° to 310°, at 31° elevation.
Last radar contact, bearing 015°, 175 miles.
The Air Force says some contacts were probably aircraft and others spurious.

records.title: Trindade Island photographs
records.place: Trindade Island, South Atlantic
records.explanation: The Brazilian Navy examined the negatives and did not declare a hoax; skeptics argue photographer Almiro Baraúna faked them.
records.shape: Saturn-like disc with a ring
records.witnesses: Crew and scientists aboard the Almirante Saldanha
records.summary: As the Navy survey ship Almirante Saldanha prepared to leave Trindade during the International Geophysical Year, people on deck saw a ringed disc approach from the east, pass over Desejado Peak, turn sharply and leave to the north-west. Photographer Almiro Baraúna took four frames; President Kubitschek allowed their release.

timeline.text: Object seen and photographed.
Photos published after Navy review.

records.title: American Airlines Captain Peter Killian’s three lights
records.place: Over central and northern Pennsylvania, between Philipsburg and Bradford
records.explanation: The Air Force first mentioned the belt of Orion, then concluded that the crew had watched three B-47s refuelling at night from KC-97 tankers, which its records placed in the area flying east to west at about 17,000 ft and 210 knots. Critics, among them NICAP and later Brad Sparks, argued that the timing and geometry do not match and that a military transport saw the lights well to the south.
records.shape: Three bright lights in a line, changing from yellow to orange, sometimes in the spacing of Orion’s belt
records.witnesses: Capt. Peter Killian and his crew, stewardesses and passengers; the crews of two other American Airlines and two United Airlines flights
records.summary: On the evening of February 24, 1959, Capt. Peter Killian, a pilot with 20,000 hours, was flying an American Airlines DC-6 from Newark to Detroit by way of Philipsburg, Bradford and Erie when he noticed three bright lights in a line off the left side of the airliner, to the south. At first he took them for the belt of Orion, then saw Orion as well. For about 45 minutes the lights stayed with the DC-6, changing colour and brightness, sometimes coming forward and sometimes falling back. Killian called two other American Airlines captains on the radio, who said they saw the lights too, and two United Airlines crews reported them in the same area; passengers and stewardesses watched. Killian filed a CIRVIS report and told the press the next day. The Air Force first mentioned Orion and then, in March, concluded that the crew had seen three B-47 bombers refuelling at night from a KC-97 tanker, a formation of lights that can last over an hour. Killian rejected it, and the case became a long-running argument between NICAP and the Air Force.

timeline.text: The DC-6 leaves Newark for Detroit.
Three lights are seen in a line south of the airliner over Pennsylvania.
The lights fall behind as the flight approaches Lake Erie.
Killian’s report is in the newspapers.
The Air Force attributes the lights to a KC-97 refuelling three B-47s.

points.note: Near Philipsburg; the lights are seen to the south

records.title: Father Gill’s sightings at Boianai
records.place: Boianai Mission, Papua (Papua New Guinea)
records.explanation: Sceptics, among them Donald Menzel, identified the first bright light as Venus and later lights as other celestial objects. Several witnesses and Gill’s own written report, signed by 25 of them, describe more than a distant light.
records.shape: Disc with figures on top; bright lights
records.witnesses: Rev. William Booth Gill and some 38 others, most of them villagers
records.summary: On the evening of June 26, 1959 the Anglican missionary William Booth Gill saw a bright white light to the north-west of the Boianai Mission. About 38 other people, mostly staff and villagers of the mission, joined him as a large disc appeared above the station, with four figures seen moving on top of it. Gill waved and, he said, the figures waved back. The sightings continued the next night. Gill wrote a report signed by 25 witnesses, and the case was studied by the Royal Australian Air Force and by J. Allen Hynek, who counted it among the best close encounters of the third kind of its time.

timeline.text: Gill sees a bright light to the north-west, then a disc over the mission.
Up to 38 people watch figures moving on the disc; one waves back.
Lights return the next evening and are watched again.
A report signed by 25 witnesses goes to the authorities; Hynek and others study the case.

records.title: Redmond, Oregon — an FAA station reports a hovering light
records.place: Redmond Airport, Redmond, Oregon
records.explanation: The Air Force first called it a balloon, then said there was insufficient information, and in 1960 Blue Book concluded that the light was the planet Venus, very bright and low in the east, distorted by refraction, possibly with Regulus. It found no evidence that the Klamath Falls radar had tracked it or that the fighters had seen anything, and a later review suggests the radar return was a false target over a gap-filler site during a temperature inversion. NICAP held that the FAA log shows radar contact and an attempted intercept.
records.shape: A bright, round, flat light that changed from white to reddish-orange, with tongues of red, yellow and green light
records.witnesses: Patrolman Robert Dickerson of the Redmond police; FAA flight service specialists at the airport
records.duration: Minutes in sight; the radar reports lasted about two hours
records.summary: Before dawn on September 24, 1959, a Redmond police officer, Robert Dickerson, saw what he first took for a falling meteor stop and hover a few hundred feet up north of the airport. FAA staff at the Redmond flight service station watched it move off to the north-east, project “long tongues of red, yellow and green light”, and, when a fast aircraft approached, rise into the clouds, then reappear to the south. The station reported it to Seattle Air Route Traffic Control Center at 1310 GMT; Seattle’s log said the Klamath Falls ground-controlled intercept radar had it, and F-102s were scrambled from Portland. Seattle later passed on radar reports of an object 25 miles from Redmond at altitudes up to 52,000 ft. The FAA’s logged account, sent to NICAP, made the case famous; the Air Force’s answers changed from a balloon to insufficient data to Venus, and in 1960 Blue Book concluded that the light was Venus and that no radar track had been confirmed.

timeline.text: Patrolman Dickerson sees a light descend and hover north of the airport.
The FAA station logs his report: the light hovers, then moves north-east.
Redmond reports to Seattle Center; the light flares and rises into cloud as a jet approaches.
Seattle Center says radar has a target 25 miles south of Redmond at 52,000 ft.
Last Seattle advisory of radar targets near Redmond.
Blue Book concludes Venus seen through refraction; no radar confirmation.

records.title: Red Bluff — California Highway Patrol sighting
records.place: Red Bluff area, Tehama County, California
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The Air Force concluded the Red Bluff sightings were due to atmospheric refraction, most probably of the planet Mars rising, with a strong temperature inversion and a layer of forest-fire smoke adding to the effect.
records.shape: Football-shaped object with red lights at each end
records.witnesses: CHP officers Charles Carson and Stanley Scott; sheriff's deputies
records.summary: Two California Highway Patrol officers thought they were about to see an airliner crash when a large object dropped toward the road ahead of them. At about 100–200 ft it stopped, reversed and climbed. They watched it for more than two hours as it moved about the sky, swept a red beam over the area and caused radio interference. Deputies at the Tehama County sheriff's office also saw lights. Similar reports came from across northern California that week.

They follow it; it sweeps a red beam and their radio suffers interference.

records.title: Betty and Barney Hill
records.place: U.S. Route 3, Franconia Notch to Indian Head, New Hampshire
records.explanation: The Air Force file notes that Jupiter was low in the south-west and would have set about when the object disappeared, and that there was a strong temperature inversion. The abduction story emerged only under hypnosis in 1964. The psychiatrist, Dr. Benjamin Simon, believed it was a fantasy that grew out of Betty's dreams.

records.witnesses: 2 (Betty and Barney Hill)
records.duration: Sighting ~1 hour; about 2 hours unaccounted for
records.summary: Driving home to Portsmouth from Montreal, the Hills saw a light moving near the Moon south of Lancaster. It followed them through Franconia Notch, passing near the Cannon Mountain tramway. South of Indian Head it came down to about 100 ft over the road, and Barney saw figures at the windows through binoculars. They reached home around dawn, about two hours later than expected. Under hypnosis in 1964 both described being taken aboard, in the first widely publicised "alien abduction".

Home in Portsmouth, about two hours later than expected.

records.place: Bahía Blanca and Espora Naval Air Base

records.title: Trancas — lights over the Moreno farm
records.place: Finca of the Moreno family beside the Belgrano railway, Trancas, Tucumán
records.shape: Several luminous objects, some over the railway line and one near the gate; a beam of light that turned violet
records.witnesses: The sisters Argentina and Yolie Moreno, the house worker Dora Martínez Guzmán, and others in the household
records.summary: At about 10 p.m. on October 21, 1963, the women of the Moreno family at their farm near Trancas, in Tucumán, saw several bright lights over the Belgrano railway line beside the property and one close to the gate. A beam from one was turned on them; it changed from white to violet, surrounded by a fog, and they felt intense heat. Figures seemed to move around the lights on the tracks. After about forty minutes the lights left in formation towards the Medina hills. The police report described a white mist with a strong smell of sulphur lasting forty minutes, and small white balls and a powder found by the tracks were later analysed as mostly calcium carbonate. The case was widely reported at the time and is one of the classic Argentine close encounters. Later local accounts add burns to the worker’s face and arm and bare ground where nothing grew; these are not in the contemporary record. La Gaceta notes that soldiers from Tucumán regiments were being moved along those tracks for exercises at the time, which could account for figures seen walking there; nobody has explained the lights.

A beam turns violet; the witnesses feel heat; figures seem to move around the lights.
The lights leave in formation towards the Medina hills.

records.witnesses: Police Sgt. Lonnie Zamora

records.title: The Solway Firth “spaceman” photograph
records.place: Burgh Marsh, near Burgh by Sands, Cumberland
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: In 2014 the researcher David Clarke concluded that the “spaceman” is most likely Templeton’s wife, Annie, who was there that day: seen from behind, her pale blue dress overexposed to white, standing beyond what the camera’s viewfinder showed. Darkened and straightened, the figure looks like a person seen from the back.
records.shape: A tall white figure in what looks like a space suit and helmet, behind the child
records.witnesses: Jim Templeton, a Carlisle fireman and photographer, his wife and their five-year-old daughter
records.duration: One photograph in a sequence of three
records.summary: On May 23, 1964, Jim Templeton photographed his five-year-old daughter Elizabeth sitting on Burgh Marsh, overlooking the Solway Firth. He said that no one else was in sight, but when the film came back the middle of three frames showed a tall white figure apparently in a space suit standing behind her. Kodak said the picture had not been tampered with, the Carlisle police found nothing suspicious, and the photograph went round the world. Templeton later told of two men claiming to be from the government who quizzed him at the marsh, and repeated a story that a Blue Streak launch at Woomera had been stopped by two similar figures. In 2014 David Clarke proposed the explanation now generally given: Templeton’s wife had walked into the background, her back to the camera, outside the part of the scene the viewfinder showed, and the overexposed blue dress turned white.

timeline.text: Templeton takes three pictures of his daughter on Burgh Marsh.

records.title: Big Sur — Atlas "Buzzing Bee" film
records.place: Anderson Peak, Big Sur, and Vandenberg AFB, California
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: Project engineer Kingston George wrote in 1993 that the film showed the re-entry vehicle releasing decoy warheads and chaff, a classified technology at the time, which Jacobs was not cleared to know about.
records.shape: Object circling a missile warhead
records.witnesses: 1369th Photographic Squadron team
records.summary: In 1964 an Air Force team on Anderson Peak used a telescope borrowed from Boston University to film Atlas missile launches from Vandenberg. In 1982, Robert Jacobs, the officer in charge on the mountain, said the film of one launch, nicknamed "Buzzing Bee", showed an object fly around the warhead and hit it with beams of light, and that the film had been confiscated. The project engineer said it showed decoy deployment.

records.title: Gemini 4 — McDivitt’s “beer can with an arm”
records.place: In orbit, passing over Hawaii, on the 20th revolution of Gemini 4
records.explanation: The likeliest explanation is a piece of the mission’s own hardware, above all the Titan II second stage that had been flying near the capsule since launch, which a NORAD officer named to Philip Klass. McDivitt accepted that one of his photographs showed the Titan stage, but always said it was not the object he had described; he called it an unknown man-made object, not an alien craft. NASA’s published picture is a different frame, which McDivitt said showed only a reflection on the window. The Condon Report listed it among three astronaut sightings it could not adequately explain.
records.shape: A white cylinder, about three times as long as it was wide, with a long arm sticking out of one side
records.witnesses: Major James McDivitt, U.S. Air Force, the command pilot; Ed White was asleep
records.summary: During the four-day flight of Gemini 4 in June 1965, with Ed White asleep beside him, James McDivitt looked out of his window while passing over Hawaii and saw a white object: “It had a very definite shape — a cylindrical object — it was white — it had a long arm that stuck out on the side.” He took two pictures and called the ground. Asked how far away it was, he guessed “ten miles or so” and added that this was only a guess, since he could not tell whether it was small and near or large and far; Mission Control said the nearest tracked object was the Pegasus satellite, about 1,200 miles away. The capsule was drifting and the window glass was dirty. He never found the frames he believed showed the object, and the picture later released as his “UFO” was one he identified as a window reflection.

timeline.text: Gemini 4 launches from Cape Kennedy; a rendezvous with the Titan stage is abandoned to save fuel.
Over Hawaii, McDivitt sees and photographs the cylinder and reports it.
Splashdown; NASA releases a frame that McDivitt says is a reflection.

records.title: Deception Island — the Antarctic sightings
records.place: Argentine station, Deception Island, South Shetland Islands
records.explanation: The Argentine Navy said in an official statement that its observers had seen a solid, lens-shaped flying object, and Lt. Daniel Perisse, at the Argentine station, said a weather balloon, a plane or a star had been ruled out. No explanation was ever published, and the photographs said to have been taken have not been released.
records.shape: Lens-shaped object, mostly red and green, changing to yellow, blue, white and orange
records.witnesses: Seventeen people at the Argentine station; nine at the Chilean station; five at the British base; two meteorologists on Laurie Island
records.summary: Over two winter nights in July 1965, the staff of three stations on Deception Island and of the Argentine station on Laurie Island, in the South Orkneys, reported a coloured, manoeuvring light. On July 2 five British observers saw a green and red light zig-zag, hover and speed up. On the evening of July 3, nine Chilean observers watched a light change colour and leave a steam-like trail, and at 19:42 seventeen people at the Argentine station, three Chilean visitors among them, watched a lens-shaped object. In a statement on July 6, the Argentine Navy described “a giant, lens-shaped flying object, solid in appearance, mostly red and green in color”, moving on a zig-zag course toward the east with changes of speed and direction, without sound, 10 to 15 km away. On Laurie Island, two variometers registered “sudden and strong disturbances of the magnetic field” during a 15-second sighting.

records.title: August 1965 — lights over Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas
records.place: Oklahoma City and across Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas and New Mexico
records.explanation: The Air Force first suggested a meteor shower, then said the lights were stars and planets made to change colour by scintillation, naming Jupiter among them. Planetarium directors in Oklahoma objected that Jupiter was not in the evening sky at that season; one suggested Antares or Vega. The reported radar contacts were never confirmed: a Tinker AFB spokesman would neither confirm nor deny them, and the base’s approach-control radar reported no contacts at the peak.
records.shape: Coloured lights, red, white and blue-green, reported hovering and moving
records.witnesses: Oklahoma Highway Patrol and police officers, weather observers and thousands of residents
records.duration: From about 8 p.m. to 3 a.m., and again the following nights
records.summary: On the night of August 1, 1965, from about 8 p.m. until 3 a.m., a steady stream of reports came in from Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas and New Mexico of coloured lights moving in the sky, some in formation. The Oklahoma Highway Patrol said officers in several towns had seen them and that Tinker Air Force Base had as many as four on radar at once at about 22,000 ft. Tinker would neither confirm nor deny the radar contacts, and its approach-control radar reported none during the height of the local sightings. The reports continued for several nights, and Blue Book received dozens from the region. The Air Force answered first that people were seeing the Delta Aquarid meteors, then that they were seeing bright stars and planets, which led to public objections from planetarium staff that the planets named were not in view.

The photos were printed in the Santa Ana Register and studied by the Air Force and the Condon Committee.

records.title: Paulding Light
records.place: Robbins Pond Road, near Paulding, Michigan
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: In May 2010 students from the optics society (SPIE) chapter at Michigan Technological University watched the light through a telescope, saw that it was a pair of car headlights, and recreated it on cue by having one of them drive U.S. 45, about 4.5 miles away, with his hazard lights on.
records.shape: A light that brightens, dims, changes colour and seems to sway
records.witnesses: Visitors to the viewing spot, nightly since the 1960s
records.summary: From the end of Robbins Pond Road in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, visitors look north along a power-line cut and see a light rise, brighten, change colour and seem to sway before going out. Teenagers first reported it in 1966, and legends grew around it, the best known being the lantern of a railway brakeman killed on the line. In 2010 a group of Michigan Tech students set up a telescope at the spot and could make out pairs of headlights, then recreated the light on cue with a car on U.S. 45, the highway that crosses the line of sight about 4.5 miles away.

records.title: The lead masks of Vintém Hill
records.place: Morro do Vintém, Niterói, Rio de Janeiro
records.explanation: The likeliest account is an accidental overdose during an attempt at contact: a friend said the men were “scientific spiritualists”, their notebook told them to take capsules and wait for a signal, and mask-making materials were found at their homes. No toxicology was ever done, so the cause of death is officially unknown.
records.shape: A round orange light rising and falling over the hill (one resident’s report)
records.witnesses: A boy who found the bodies; police; a local resident who reported an orange light
records.summary: On August 17, 1966, two electronics technicians from Campos dos Goytacazes, Manoel Pereira da Cruz and Miguel José Viana, travelled to Niterói, bought raincoats and a bottle of water, and were last seen in a bar, one of them nervously checking his watch. On August 20 a boy flying a kite on Morro do Vintém found their bodies side by side, dressed in suits and raincoats, with crude lead eye-masks beside them. There were no signs of violence. A notebook held the instructions “16:30 be at the specified place. 18:30 swallow capsules, after the effect protect metals, await signal, mask”. The autopsy came weeks late and no toxicology was done, so the cause of death was never established. Days after the discovery, Rio newspapers reported that a resident had seen a round orange object rising and falling over the hill on the night the men went up, and the case entered UFO literature through Flying Saucer Review in 1967. There is no evidence linking the light to the deaths; a friend told police the men belonged to a group of “scientific spiritualists” who tried to contact other beings, which points to drugs taken in a ritual.

timeline.text: The two men arrive in Niterói by bus and buy raincoats and water.
The time their notebook set for taking the capsules.
A resident later says she saw an orange light over Morro do Vintém.
A boy flying a kite finds the bodies; police reach them the next day.
A late autopsy finds no injuries; no toxicology is done.

records.witnesses: Launch crew; security guards (later testimony)
records.summary: All ten Minuteman I missiles of Echo Flight dropped off strategic alert almost simultaneously. Decades later, former missile officers said guards had reported a glowing red object hovering at the gate. The Air Force’s contemporaneous report found no UFO involvement.

records.place: Falcon Lake, Whiteshell Provincial Park, Manitoba
records.explanation: RCMP, RCAF and the Condon Committee could not explain it; some soil samples were mildly radioactive, possibly from radium paint. Later marks on Michalak’s body were judged self-inflicted.
records.shape: Two glowing oval objects; one landed
records.witnesses: Stefan Michalak
records.summary: Amateur prospector Stefan Michalak said two glowing craft descended near him; one landed on a rock outcrop. When he touched it, a blast of hot gas from a grid-like vent burned his chest. CBC has called it Canada’s best-documented UFO case.

records.title: UMMO — the San José de Valderas photographs
records.place: San José de Valderas, Alcorcón, near Madrid
records.explanation: A hoax. José Luis Jordán Peña, the main witness of the 1966 Aluche “landing”, admitted in the 1990s that he had invented UMMO as an experiment in credulity and that the photographs showed a small model hung from nylon thread; a stylistic study of the letters signed “Antonio Pardo” pointed to him, and in 1996 Manuel Carballal reproduced the pictures with a model on a fishing line.
records.shape: A circular craft with the UMMO sign, )+(, on its underside
records.witnesses: Anonymous photographers (“Antonio Pardo”); no credible eyewitnesses were found
records.duration: A few minutes, according to the photographers
records.summary: In June 1967 photographs of a round craft marked underneath with the sign )+( reached the Madrid newspaper Informaciones and Spanish UFO researchers, left anonymously at a photo shop in Carabanchel and sent by a man signing himself “Antonio Pardo”. They were said to have been taken on June 1 at San José de Valderas, outside Madrid. The sign was that of UMMO, a planet whose inhabitants had been writing long typed letters to Spanish enthusiasts since the mid-1960s, and the pictures made UMMO famous. No reliable witness of the flight was ever found; the negatives that were later analysed had gaps in their sequence, and a police laboratory study in the 1990s, while finding no thread, noted lighting that suggested artificial light and could not rule out fraud. In the 1990s José Luis Jordán Peña, a Madrid engineer with an interest in parapsychology, admitted that he had created UMMO, that he had written the letters with the help of a few friends, and that the photographs showed a model hung from a thread. Believers still defend the case.

timeline.text: Jordán Peña and another witness report a landing at Aluche, Madrid.
The date given for the San José de Valderas photographs.
Prints reach Informaciones and researchers from anonymous photographers.
Jordán Peña confesses to inventing UMMO; the photos used a model on a thread.
Manuel Carballal reproduces the photographs with a model on a fishing line.

records.witnesses: François (13) and his sister Anne-Marie (9)
records.summary: On August 29, 1967 a 13-year-old boy, François, and his 9-year-old sister, Anne-Marie, told the local police that while watching cows in a field at Cussac they had seen four small black beings, about 120 cm tall, with a shiny, silk-like look. The police noted a smell of sulphur and dried grass at the spot the craft was said to have left. The file is one of those that the French government put online in March 2007, and one of the children was later said to have suffered lasting health effects.

records.title: Six “flying saucers” across southern England (hoax)
records.place: A line of six sites from the Isle of Sheppey, Kent, to Clevedon, Somerset
records.explanation: A Rag Week hoax by aircraft engineering apprentices at the Royal Aircraft Establishment, Farnborough, led by Christopher Southall and Roger Palmer: fibreglass shells with an oscillator and loudspeaker inside, filled with fermenting flour paste. They owned up the same day and raised money for charity.
records.shape: Smooth, metallic-looking saucers about 1.4 m long, emitting a bleeping noise
records.witnesses: Members of the public who found them; four police forces, army bomb-disposal teams, the RAF and the MoD
records.summary: On the morning of Monday, September 4, 1967, people in southern England began finding small “flying saucers”, six in all, set out along a nearly straight line at about 51.5° N: on a housing estate near Queenborough on the Isle of Sheppey, on a golf course in Bromley, in a paddock at Winkfield near Ascot, at Welford near Newbury, at Chippenham, and on Dial Hill at Clevedon. Each was about 1.4 m long, weighed about 45 kg and gave out an eerie electronic sound. Police cordoned them off; army bomb-disposal teams, RAF helicopters and the Ministry of Defence’s intelligence staff were called in; the army blew up the Chippenham saucer, one was lifted from Sheppey by helicopter, and one was sent to the Atomic Weapons Research Establishment at Aldermaston. When one was drilled into, a foul-smelling paste burst out over the police. By the evening the makers, apprentices from the Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough, had owned up: it was a stunt for their Rag Week. The MoD’s file on the day was released by The National Archives.

Teams place six saucers along a line across southern England.

records.title: Zond IV re-entry — the “craft with windows”
records.place: Across the sky from Kentucky through Ohio to Pennsylvania
records.explanation: NORAD identified the objects as fragments of the Soviet Zond IV probe or its rocket re-entering the atmosphere; Blue Book closed the case as satellite decay. The Condon study used it as its standard example of how honest witnesses turn a re-entry into a structured craft.
records.shape: Two or three fiery objects with golden-orange tails; some witnesses described a cigar-shaped craft with lit windows
records.witnesses: Hundreds of people along a line from Kentucky to Pennsylvania; about 78 written reports
records.summary: At about 9:45 p.m. EST on March 3, 1968, hundreds of people along a line from Kentucky to Pennsylvania saw a slow procession of fiery objects with golden-orange tails cross the sky to the north-east. Most saw two or three main pieces; some described a single long, wingless craft, said that “many windows seemed to be lit up from the inside”, or put it at treetop level. NORAD identified the objects as pieces of the Soviet Zond IV probe, launched on March 2, or of its rocket, and Project Blue Book recorded “satellite decay”; a contractor even estimated where surviving pieces might have fallen in north-central Pennsylvania. For the Condon study, William Hartmann compared about 30 detailed reports with the known event: many put the objects within a few miles and below 10,000 ft, when the debris was burning up tens of kilometres high, and the joining of separate lights into one windowed hull became his textbook case of the “airship effect”.

timeline.text: Zond IV is launched from Baikonur on a Proton rocket.
Fiery objects cross the sky from Kentucky towards Pennsylvania, heading north-east.
Reports reach Blue Book and the Colorado project; some describe a windowed craft at low altitude.
NORAD identifies the objects as Zond IV debris; Blue Book closes the file as satellite decay.
The identification is confirmed.
The Condon report publishes Hartmann’s comparison of the reports with the re-entry.

records.explanation: Blue Book's conclusion: ground sightings were probably the B-52 and the star Sirius; the radar contact and the B-52's temporary loss of UHF radio were "possibly plasma", similar to ball lightning; the crew's sighting could have been the star Vega or a light on the ground.
records.shape: Large glowing orange object
records.witnesses: Missile maintenance and security teams; B-52 crew
records.summary: Before dawn, maintenance and security teams at several Minuteman sites reported a large glowing object. A B-52 returning to Minot was asked to look for it. Its radar navigator painted a target that stayed about a mile off the bomber, and radarscope photographs were taken. The UHF radio dropped out when the object was closest. After landing, the crew described a bright light near the ground. Blue Book closed it within weeks. It is one of the best-documented military cases in the files.

B-52 radar paints a target about 1 mile off; radarscope photos taken.
UHF radio transmissions fail during the closest approach.
On approach, the crew sees a bright light near the ground.

records.title: Jimmy Carter’s light at Leary, Georgia
records.place: Outside the Lions Club meeting, Leary, Georgia
records.explanation: Robert Sheaffer and Allan Hendry identified it as Venus, which was near its greatest brilliancy in the western sky that evening; a later analysis proposed a barium-cloud release from a rocket fired at Eglin AFB. Carter himself said he never thought it was an alien craft.
records.shape: A bright light, as bright as the Moon, changing from white to blue to red and back
records.witnesses: Jimmy Carter, then a Georgia state senator and Lions Club district governor, and about ten others
records.summary: At about 7:15 one evening in 1969, Jimmy Carter was waiting outside a school lunchroom in Leary, Georgia, to speak to the local Lions Club, when one of the men pointed out a light in the west, about 30 degrees above the horizon. Carter said it seemed to come closer, stopped beyond the pine trees, changed from white to blue, then red, then white, and then receded, after 10 to 12 minutes. As governor, in September 1973, he filled in a sighting report for the International UFO Bureau, dating it October 1969; the Lions Club’s own records show his Leary speech was on January 6, 1969, and the club had disbanded before October. Investigators in 1976 found that most of those present did not remember the event. On January 6, Venus was a brilliant evening star in the direction Carter gave, which is the accepted explanation; Carter said later that he took it for something unexplained, not for a spacecraft.

timeline.text: A light is pointed out in the western sky; it brightens, changes colour and recedes.
Governor Carter signs a report for the International UFO Bureau, dated “October 1969”.
Investigators find the Lions Club speech was on January 6, 1969; few witnesses remember it.
Robert Sheaffer publishes the Venus identification.

The story went around the world. Rumours said the army investigated the site but no records were produced. The town's "UFO Bar" and hotel clippings kept the story alive.

records.title: Delphos ring
records.place: Delphos, Kansas
records.explanation: No official body reached a conclusion. The soil results are the main physical evidence; sceptics note that the account rests on one family, and that fungi can leave rings of altered, water-repelling soil.
records.shape: Mushroom-shaped, with multicoloured lights
records.witnesses: Ronnie Johnson (16) and his parents
records.summary: While doing evening chores on his family’s farm near Delphos, 16-year-old Ronnie Johnson saw a mushroom-shaped object, lit in many colours, hovering about 25 yards away. His parents came out to a glowing ring on the ground where it had been. It was still visible the next day. Investigators found that the soil in the ring was dry beside damp ground and would not let water through, and that it held more calcium and soluble salts and was more acidic, with a white deposit of calcium oxalate. Both calcium oxalate and oxalic acid irritate skin and eyes, and Ronnie’s parents said touching the ring numbed their fingers. It is one of the classic UFO “landing trace” cases.

timeline.text: Ronnie sees a mushroom-shaped, multicoloured object hovering about 25 yards away.
A glowing ring is seen on the ground where it hovered.
The ring is still visible; investigators take soil samples.
Soil analyses find water-resistant, acidic soil with calcium oxalate.

records.title: Pascagoula encounter
records.place: Pascagoula River, Pascagoula, Mississippi
records.explanation: No physical evidence was found beyond the two men’s testimony. Sceptics see a hoax or a hallucination; the witnesses stuck to their story, including when they were secretly recorded at the sheriff’s office.
records.shape: Oval object with flashing blue lights
records.witnesses: Charles Hickson (45) and Calvin Parker (17)
records.summary: Charles Hickson and his young colleague Calvin Parker said that while fishing from a pier on the west bank of the Pascagoula River they heard a whirring noise, saw two flashing blue lights and an oval object about 30–40 feet across, and were taken aboard by three creatures with claw-like hands, examined and returned. They went to the Jackson County sheriff’s office around 11 p.m. Officers who suspected a prank left the two alone in a room with a hidden recorder; the men’s talk matched their story. The case set off a wave of 1973 reports along the Gulf Coast and made Hickson a long-time public speaker; Parker published his own account in 2018.

timeline.text: Hickson and Parker fish from a pier and see blue lights and an oval craft.
They report to the Jackson County sheriff’s office.
Officers record the two men alone in a room; their talk matches their story.
The story spreads across the U.S. and sparks a wave of Gulf Coast reports.

records.title: Coyne helicopter incident
records.place: Near Mansfield, Ohio
records.explanation: The sceptic Philip Klass argued that the crew first saw a bright fireball of the Orionid meteor shower and then misjudged what followed. Investigators for CUFOS and others reject this: by their timeline the object was in view for several minutes, and a family on the ground reported lights too.
records.shape: Grey cigar-shaped body, red nose light, white tail light, green beam
records.witnesses: Four-man Army Reserve crew; a family on the ground
records.summary: An Army Reserve Bell UH-1H (tail number 68-15444) on its way from Columbus to Cleveland was cruising at 2,500 feet near Mansfield when the crew saw a red light closing on the helicopter from the east. Capt. Lawrence Coyne took the controls and began an emergency descent, expecting a collision. They then saw a cigar-shaped grey object hover over the helicopter, with a red light at the nose, a white light at the tail and a green beam that lit the cockpit. After it left, the crew found the helicopter at about 3,500 feet in a climb of 1,000 feet a minute, with the collective still fully down, and the compass spinning. The Army Reserve’s report is among the best-known official records of an aircrew encounter.

timeline.text: The UH-1H leaves Columbus for Cleveland.
A red light is seen closing from the east; Coyne descends from 2,500 to 1,700 ft.
A grey, cigar-shaped object hovers over the helicopter; a green beam fills the cockpit.
The object leaves to the west; the helicopter is found at ~3,500 ft, climbing, compass spinning.

points.note: Red light seen to the east

records.title: Berwyn Mountains "crash"
records.place: Cadair Berwyn, North Wales
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: A small earthquake shook the area at the same moment that a bright fireball was seen across northern England and Wales. The lights on the hillside were most likely poachers' lamps. Investigators found no crash and no recovery.
records.shape: Glowing light on the hillside
records.witnesses: Villagers across the Dee valley; a nurse who drove up the mountain
records.summary: At 20:38 a loud bang and tremor shook villages around the Berwyn Mountains, and people saw lights on the hillside. A local nurse drove up and described a glowing sphere. Police searched and found nothing. The event was later retold as a UFO crash with a secret military recovery, sometimes called "the Welsh Roswell". Seismographs recorded an earthquake, and meteor observers logged a fireball at the same moment.

timeline.text: Bang and tremor felt across the region; seismographs register an earthquake.
Bright fireball seen over northern England and Wales.
Nurse drives up the mountain and sees a glowing light; police search.

records.title: The Betz mystery sphere
records.place: Fort George Island, Jacksonville, Florida
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: The Navy, which examined the ball in April 1974, said it was “nothing more than a huge ball bearing”, a stainless-steel ball used as a check valve in industrial piping, and its size, weight and steel match such a valve. An artist later said a few of these balls, which he used in sculptures, fell off his van’s roof rack near Jacksonville around 1971. It “moved on its own” only after being handled; a Navy man pointed to the house’s old, uneven stone floors and the ball’s near-perfect balance.
records.shape: A heavy, polished metal ball about 20 cm across
records.witnesses: Antoine, Jerri and Terry Betz; the U.S. Navy at Jacksonville; reporters
records.duration: Found in an afternoon; the stories ran for weeks
records.summary: On March 27, 1974, the Betz family went to look at a small brush fire near their home on Fort George Island and found a shiny metal sphere about 8 inches (20 cm) across, weighing about 22 lb (10 kg), They took it for a conquistadors’ cannonball and kept it. Two weeks later their son Terry was playing the guitar near it and said it answered with a throbbing hum; the family went on to say it rolled across the floor, stopped and turned by itself, and seemed to follow people around the house. The story went national, the National Enquirer offered a reward for proof that anything was from outer space, and the Navy took the ball for tests: it was hollow, with a shell about half an inch thick, and made of stainless steel. A panel of scientists at an Enquirer conference in June agreed it was “made on earth”.

timeline.text: The family finds the sphere near a brush fire.
It hums to Terry’s guitar and is said to roll by itself.
The Navy examines it and calls it a huge ball bearing.
Scientists at an Enquirer conference say it was made on Earth.
Skeptoid matches it to a commercial check-valve ball.

records.title: Coyame “crash” — Chihuahua
records.place: Coyame, Chihuahua, Mexico
records.explanation: Historians say the reports were most likely prompted by the crash and military recovery of a Cessna used for drug smuggling. The radar story that circulates in UFO literature is known only from later retellings.
records.shape: Disc-shaped object (as told)
records.witnesses: Local residents (reported)
records.summary: According to ufologists, residents near Coyame, in the Chihuahuan desert, reported a mid-air collision between a UFO and a small aeroplane on August 25, 1974, followed by a military recovery and a cover-up. The best-known version says U.S. air-defence radar followed a fast, high object from the Gulf of Mexico until it vanished near Coyame, and that a light aircraft that had left El Paso collided with it. Historians point instead to the real 1974 crash and recovery of a Cessna that had been carrying drugs, which they believe gave rise to the story. It is sometimes called Mexico’s Roswell. The case is listed because it is so often cited, not because the account is documented.

timeline.text: In the later retellings, radar follows a fast object toward Chihuahua.
Residents report a collision between the object and a small aeroplane near Coyame.
A military recovery and cover-up are alleged. Historians identify a crashed drug-smuggling Cessna.

records.place: Langenburg, Saskatchewan

records.summary: Farmer Edwin Fuhr was swathing a rapeseed field when he saw five metallic, dome-shaped objects spinning just above the ground near a slough. He sat frozen for about 15 minutes until they rose silently in formation and left, trailing grey vapour. He said his swather would not restart. The RCMP found five rings of flattened, swirled crop matching his description, with no tracks leading in.

records.title: Billy Meier’s “beamship” photographs
records.place: Zürcher Oberland, around Hinwil, canton of Zürich
records.explanation: A hoax. Meier’s former wife said in 1997 that the “beamships” were models made from household objects such as dustbin lids and carpet tacks; Meier admitted to Gary Kinder that he had used models to “recreate scenes”; and photographs of two “Pleiadian” women turned out to show dancers from the Golddiggers troupe on The Dean Martin Show.
records.shape: Disc-shaped “beamships” with domes and rings
records.witnesses: Eduard “Billy” Meier alone; no independent witness of any contact
records.summary: Eduard “Billy” Meier, from the canton of Zürich, says that on January 28, 1975, he met Semjase, a woman from the Pleiades, beside her spacecraft, and that contacts which had begun in his childhood went on for years. From 1975 he produced hundreds of sharp colour photographs and some film of saucer-shaped “beamships” over the fields and woods of the Zürcher Oberland, later the basis of books, a following and the 1987 film Contact. Scientists, sceptics and most ufologists regard them as fraudulent. Investigators such as Kal Korff argued that models had been photographed close up or combined with landscapes; Meier’s former wife Kalliope said in 1997 that she had seen the models and that the stories were invented; Meier conceded that he had used models to re-create scenes; and pictures he presented as the aliens Asket and Nera were traced to performers on American television.

timeline.text: Meier says his contacts with the Pleiadian Semjase begin.
He produces hundreds of photographs and some film of “beamships”.
The film Contact presents his story without critics.

records.title: Loring Air Force Base intrusions
records.place: Loring Air Force Base, Limestone, Maine
records.explanation: The Air Force never identified the object; its messages from the base describe an unidentified, helicopter-like aircraft that evaded the ground sweep. No conventional aircraft was found.
records.shape: Low aircraft with a red light and a white strobe
records.witnesses: Security police, including S/Sgt Danny Lewis
records.duration: About 40 minutes the first night; repeated for days
records.summary: On the evening of October 27, 1975 a security patrol at Loring Air Force Base, a Strategic Air Command base that held nuclear weapons, saw an aircraft with a red light and a white strobe approaching the north perimeter at about 300 feet. The base was put on alert and a ground sweep began. Over the next 40 minutes the object came within 300 yards of the restricted weapons storage area at about 150 feet, moving in ways described as helicopter-like, and no one could get a fix on it before it left toward Grand Falls, New Brunswick. Similar reports came from the base, and from other bases, for more than a week; Air Force messages about them were released under the Freedom of Information Act.

timeline.text: A patrol sees a low aircraft with a red light and a white strobe near the north perimeter.
The base goes on alert; the object comes within 300 yards of the weapons storage area.
It leaves toward Grand Falls, New Brunswick, without being identified.
More sightings are logged at Loring and other northern bases.

records.title: Wurtsmith Air Force Base and the KC-135 chase
records.place: Wurtsmith Air Force Base, Oscoda, Michigan
records.explanation: The NORAD log called it a helicopter over the weapons storage area, but no helicopter was identified, and the tanker crew described an object that pulled away each time they closed on it. It is one of a series of intrusions at northern Strategic Air Command bases that autumn, including Loring and Malmstrom.
records.shape: One white light pointing down and two red lights at the rear
records.witnesses: Base security police and the six-man crew of a KC-135 tanker
records.summary: At about 10:10 p.m. on October 30, 1975, guards at Wurtsmith, a Strategic Air Command base on Lake Huron, saw an object with a white light pointing downward and two red lights at the rear. Minutes later security police reported an “unidentified helicopter” hovering low over the weapons storage area, and the base radar approach control picked up a target about 35 miles to the south-east. A KC-135 tanker flying nearby was asked to look. Its six-man crew, among them Maj. Frederick Pappas, saw lights and painted the object on their radar for about ten seconds, and followed it at about 2,000 feet north over Lake Huron and then south toward Saginaw Bay; each time they closed in it sped away, and Capt. Myron Taylor put its final speed at about 1,000 knots. Low on fuel, they broke off. The NORAD log recorded that the tanker “made both visual sighting and radar skin paint” and that contact was lost 25 nautical miles south-east over Lake Huron.

timeline.text: Guards see a white downward light and two red lights; others see lights at the western edge of the base.
Security police report an unlit “helicopter” hovering over the weapons storage area.
Radar approach control tracks a target about 35 miles south-east.
The KC-135 chases it north over Lake Huron, then south toward Saginaw Bay, and paints it on radar.
Contact is lost; the object is seen once more before the tanker, short of fuel, breaks off.

records.title: Travis Walton disappearance
records.place: Apache–Sitgreaves National Forest near Heber, Arizona
records.explanation: The crew passed some polygraph tests and Walton failed one. Philip Klass and Michael Shermer argued it was a hoax, with a motive: the crew was behind on a Forest Service contract, and an "act of God" could excuse the penalty. Walton maintains it happened.
records.shape: Glowing disc hovering over a clearing
records.witnesses: 7 (the logging crew)
records.summary: A seven-man logging crew led by Mike Rogers was driving out of the forest after sunset when they saw a glowing disc over a clearing. Travis Walton got out and walked toward it, and the crew said a beam of light knocked him to the ground. They drove off in panic. When they came back he was gone. Police searched for five days. Walton then called his sister from a phone booth in Heber, saying he had been taken aboard. His story became the 1993 film Fire in the Sky.

Crew reports to the Navajo County sheriff; searches begin.

records.title: Malmstrom AFB — objects over the missile fields, November 1975
records.place: Malmstrom Air Force Base and its Minuteman missile fields, Montana
records.shape: Lights over the launch facilities; on radar, slow targets that sounded like a jet
records.witnesses: Missile-site security teams, Air Defense radar operators and F-106 crews
records.summary: In the first weeks of November 1975, after the intrusions at Loring and Wurtsmith, NORAD’s logs and messages record a run of reports from the Minuteman fields around Malmstrom AFB in Montana. Security teams at several launch facilities reported lights and objects; Malmstrom’s search and height-finder radars carried a target between about 9,000 and 15,600 ft moving at only seven knots; witnesses said it sounded like a jet, and the FAA said no jets were in the area. F-106 interceptors scrambled from Malmstrom could not make contact because of the darkness and the target’s low altitude. The NORAD messages, released under the Freedom of Information Act by 1979, give no explanation. Later accounts add a security alarm at launch facility K-7, a glowing disc “the size of a football field” and tampered warheads; those details come from interviews years afterwards, not from the released records.

timeline.text: Intrusions at Loring and Wurtsmith air force bases.
Malmstrom radars and missile-site teams report objects; F-106s are scrambled and see nothing.
A NORAD message summarises the Malmstrom sightings.
The NORAD logs are released under FOIA and published.
More of the records are released by the Office of the Secretary of Defense (FOIA 97-F-1677).

records.title: CFS Falconbridge — the NORAD message from Ontario
records.place: 30 nautical miles south-south-west of Canadian Forces Station Falconbridge, near Sudbury, Ontario
records.explanation: No explanation was given. The sighting came in the autumn of 1975, when bases along the northern U.S. border were also reporting lights and radar targets. The radar fixed only a bearing and range; the height and the vertical climb are the observers’ estimates.
records.shape: A circular, brilliantly lit object with two black spots in the centre
records.witnesses: Four members of the station (a major, a captain, a corporal and a master corporal); many reports to the Ontario Provincial Police in Sudbury
records.summary: At 11:15 UTC (6:15 a.m. local) on November 11, 1975, personnel at CFS Falconbridge, a Pinetree Line radar station north-east of Sudbury, saw and tracked an object bearing 210 degrees magnetic, 30 nautical miles from the station. 22nd NORAD Region Headquarters passed the report to the National Research Council in Ottawa: a “circular object, brilliantly lighted with two black spots in the center”, moving straight up “at high speed from 42,000 ft. to 72,000 ft.” with no horizontal movement, for 14 minutes, under broken cloud. The major who was the prime witness took photographs but did not know if they would come out. The same observers saw a similar object bearing 270 degrees, too far away for detail, and the Ontario Provincial Police in Sudbury received many other reports. The station’s history adds that two F-106 interceptors were scrambled from Selfridge Air National Guard Base in Michigan and saw nothing.

It rises from about 42,000 to 72,000 ft with no horizontal movement.

Two F-106s from Selfridge ANGB find nothing.

records.title: Canary Islands sphere
records.place: Canary Islands (Gran Canaria, Tenerife, Fuerteventura)
records.explanation: Spanish researcher Ricardo Campo matched the 1976 sighting, and similar Canary Islands events of the period, to U.S. Navy submarine-launched Poseidon missile tests in the Atlantic, whose exhaust clouds glow in sunlight at high altitude. The Spanish Air Force report left it unexplained.
records.shape: Light rising from the sea, then a huge glowing sphere
records.witnesses: Several hundred, including the crew of the Spanish Navy corvette Atrevida
records.summary: The crew of the corvette Atrevida saw a light rise from the sea, then a vast, luminous sphere spread out in the sky. Hundreds of people across Tenerife, La Palma, La Gomera and Gran Canaria saw it. A doctor near Gáldar said he saw two tall figures inside a transparent sphere. The Spanish Air Force investigation was leaked in 1977 and officially declassified in 1994.

timeline.text: Corvette Atrevida sees a light rise and a glowing halo expand.
Sphere seen across the islands; photographs taken.
Journalist J. J. Benítez publishes the Air Force report.
Report officially declassified.

records.title: The Allagash abductions
records.place: Eagle Lake, Allagash Wilderness Waterway, northern Maine
records.explanation: The abduction rests on memories recovered under hypnosis years later, a method that is known to produce false memories. The four agree that they saw a bright light over the lake and that their fire had burned down sooner than they expected; the rest is in dispute. In 2016 Chuck Rak said the abduction “didn’t happen”, that he had backed the story to make money and that they had been “stoned” on the lake; Charlie Foltz and Jim Weiner deny the drugs and stand by it.
records.shape: A large glowing sphere that changed colour and shone a beam on the water
records.witnesses: Jim and Jack Weiner and Chuck Rak, art students, and their guide Charlie Foltz
records.duration: Minutes as they remember it; hours by the fire
records.summary: In late August 1976 four young men from Massachusetts were on a canoe trip in the Allagash wilderness. On the night of August 26, camped by Eagle Lake, they built a big bonfire as a landmark and paddled out to fish in the dark. They say a bright sphere rose over the trees, and when Rak signalled at it with a flashlight it came toward them and shone a beam down on the water; the next thing they knew they were back on the shore, and the fire that should have burned for hours was embers. Years later the ufologist Raymond Fowler took up the case, and under hypnosis all four described being taken aboard and examined. Fowler’s 1993 book The Allagash Abductions made it one of the best-known abduction cases, and one of the few claimed by a whole group.

timeline.text: Fishing on Eagle Lake, they see a light; the fire has burned down when they return.
Raymond Fowler arranges hypnotic regressions of all four.
Fowler publishes The Allagash Abductions.
Chuck Rak tells a Maine newspaper the abduction did not happen.

records.title: Tehran F-4 Phantom intercepts
records.place: Tehran, Iran
records.explanation: A U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency report called it "an outstanding report" meeting all criteria for a valid study. Skeptic Philip Klass proposed Jupiter plus coincidental equipment failures.
records.shape: Brilliant flashing lights; object released a smaller one
records.witnesses: Controllers, two F-4 crews, a general, civilians
records.summary: After civilian reports of a bright object over Tehran’s Shemiran district, the Imperial Iranian Air Force scrambled two F-4 Phantoms from Shahrokhi AB. Both crews said their instruments and communications failed near the object; the second pilot, Maj. Parviz Jafari, reported a radar lock and that his weapons panel died as a smaller object came toward him.

First F-4 (Lt. Nazeri) launches; loses instruments at 25 nmi and returns.
Second F-4 (Maj. Jafari) launches; radar lock at 27 nmi.
Smaller object launches toward the F-4; AIM-9 panel fails.
DIA evaluation memo distributed.

records.title: The Moroccan coast “UFO” — a Soviet rocket part re-entering
records.place: Along the Atlantic coast of Morocco, from Agadir to Kenitra and inland to Meknes and Fez
records.explanation: In 2012 the satellite tracker Ted Molczan matched the time and track to the re-entry of a piece of a Soviet Molniya rocket (an ullage-motor assembly from the third stage that orbited Molniya 1-35 in July 1976), an object catalogued by U.S. space tracking. The State Department’s 1976 reply had already said the sightings “could conceivably be compatible with a meteor, or a decaying satellite”. The witnesses’ estimate of 1,000 m was far too low, as estimates of a re-entry’s height usually are.
records.shape: A silvery, luminous flattened ball or a large luminous tube, shedding bright sparks from the rear
records.witnesses: People in Agadir, Kalaa Sraghna, Essaouira, Casablanca, Rabat, Kenitra, Meknes and around Fez, including Maj. Mohamed Lissaoui of the Royal Gendarmerie
records.summary: Between 1 and 2 a.m. on September 19, 1976, the Royal Gendarmerie took calls from Agadir, Marrakech, Casablanca, Rabat, Kenitra and other towns describing the same thing: a silent, silvery, luminous object, disc-shaped to some and tube-shaped to others, moving slowly from south to north parallel to the Atlantic coast and giving off intermittent trails of bright sparks and fragments. Major Mohamed Lissaoui of the Gendarmerie saw it himself at about 1:15 a.m. on his way back from Kenitra, flying low and slowly “as if it were an aircraft preparing to land”. King Hassan II sent the Gendarmerie’s commander, Col. Housni Benslimane, to the U.S. embassy on September 23 to ask what the Americans knew; the defence attaché was shown witnesses’ drawings and cabled Washington. The State Department answered that it knew of no U.S. aircraft or satellite activity and that a meteor or a decaying satellite was possible. The cables became public through WikiLeaks in 2013.

records.title: Broad Haven schoolchildren — the Welsh Triangle
records.place: Broad Haven, Pembrokeshire, Wales
records.explanation: A Ministry of Defence investigator found no physical evidence that anything had landed and suggested that “a local prankster” might have been responsible. The children’s drawings agreed closely, which is why the case is still told.
records.shape: Yellow cigar-shaped craft; later an “upside-down saucer”
records.witnesses: 14 schoolchildren, then teachers and a hotel owner
records.duration: Lunchtime on Feb 4; further reports to April
records.summary: At lunchtime on February 4, 1977 a group of 14 children at Broad Haven Primary School reported a yellow, cigar-shaped craft that landed in a field beyond the school grounds, and a silver creature with pointed ears. The headmaster had them draw what they saw, and the drawings agreed closely. On February 17 teachers and others said they saw the same craft, and on April 19 the owner of the Haven Fort Hotel in nearby Little Haven reported an “upside-down saucer” and two figures in a field. The wave of sightings in the area became known as the Dyfed or Welsh Triangle. A Ministry of Defence investigator found nothing to show a landing. The events were revisited in a 2023 Netflix documentary and a 2024 BBC series.

The headmaster asks them to draw it; the drawings match closely.
Teachers and other witnesses report the same craft.

records.title: Corporal Valdés — the patrol at Pampa Lluscuma
records.place: Pampa Lluscuma, near Putre, Arica
records.explanation: Valdés himself said in later interviews (reported for 2004, 2009 and 2013) that it was a joke among the patrol that got out of hand, with the watch set forward and the beard explained away to avoid punishment for not shaving, though at other times he has said it happened. The army never investigated and the watch was never examined.
records.shape: Bright violet lights descending from the sky
records.witnesses: Corporal Armando Valdés Garrido and seven conscripts of a Chilean Army patrol
records.summary: In the early hours of April 25, 1977, a Chilean Army patrol of a corporal and seven conscripts camped on the Pampa Lluscuma, in the altiplano near Putre, said two bright lights came down near them. Corporal Armando Valdés walked towards one and disappeared; about fifteen minutes later he came back, collapsed and said, “You don’t know who we are or where we come from, but I assure you we will return.” The soldiers said his face now carried several days’ beard and his digital watch showed a date five days ahead. The story reached the press across the world, from Chilean papers to French ones, and became Chile’s best-known UFO case. It was never investigated under the military government: no statement was taken officially and the watch was neither photographed nor studied. Later reporting found that the group was guarding army horses rather than patrolling, and some soldiers said Valdés had a beard before that night. Valdés has given contradictory accounts since, at times calling it a prank that got out of hand.

timeline.text: The patrol sees bright lights descend; Valdés walks towards one and vanishes.
He returns, collapses and speaks of “they” returning; the soldiers notice a beard and the watch’s date.
The story spreads through Chilean and foreign newspapers.

records.place: Colares Island, Pará

records.shape: Beams of light, "chupa-chupa" lights
records.witnesses: Islanders; Brazilian Air Force team
records.summary: Residents of Colares reported lights that fired beams and left burn-like marks. The mayor asked for help, and the Brazilian Air Force ran Operação Prato under Capt. Uyrangê Hollanda, photographing lights over several months. Hollanda gave a dramatic interview two decades later.

records.title: The object that fell near Bermejo — Bolivia’s 1978 search
records.place: El Taire hill above the Bermejo River, Tarija department, on the Argentine border
records.shape: A luminous cylinder or egg with a flaming tail
records.witnesses: Many people along the border; Bolivian Air Force pilots who searched the slope
records.duration: Seconds (the fall), followed by an explosion
records.summary: In the afternoon of May 6, 1978 (some reports say the Sunday evening, May 7), people on both sides of the Bermejo River, where Bolivia’s Tarija department meets Argentina, saw a luminous object with a fiery tail fall towards the El Taire hill and heard an explosion and a sonic boom. The Bolivian army and police searched, scientists from the University of Tarija went to the area, Argentina sent border police, and newspapers in Buenos Aires carried a police chief’s description of a dull metal cylinder about four metres long. The U.S. Embassy in La Paz reported the fall to Washington, and two U.S. Air Force attachés flew to Tarija; the embassy denied any secret recovery. A CIA-released bulletin of May 17, 1978 is headed “Bolivia reports conflict on details of fallen object”. The searches, slowed by the terrain and weather, recovered nothing anyone published. Explanations at the time ranged from a meteorite to space debris; no country reported losing a satellite, no meteorite fall is catalogued there for that date, and the object was never identified.

timeline.text: A fiery object falls towards El Taire; an explosion and a boom are heard far away.
Bolivian army, police and university teams search; Argentina sends border police.

A CIA bulletin notes conflicting Bolivian reports about the object.
Nothing is recovered; the object is never identified.

records.title: Gujan-Mestras — the light that put out the street lamps
records.place: Gujan-Mestras, Arcachon basin, Gironde
records.statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
records.explanation: GEIPAN class B: the witnesses probably saw an atmospheric phenomenon linked to the thunderstorm threatening the area. The gendarmerie and GEPAN could not link the town sighting to a light seen by motorists near La Réole.
records.shape: An orange, oval luminous object
records.witnesses: Several residents; motorists on the RN113 near La Réole
records.summary: On the night of June 19, 1978, several people in Gujan-Mestras, on the Arcachon basin, heard a loud, dull noise and then saw an orange, oval light over the town. While it was there the street lighting faltered; the light faded from view as it climbed. Motorists on the road to Bordeaux near La Réole also saw a light moving slowly in the stormy sky. The gendarmerie took statements and GEPAN, the French space agency’s UFO office, investigated. GEIPAN classes the case B: probably a weather phenomenon connected with the storm. The two sightings could not be shown to be the same thing.

records.title: Kuwait’s oil-field sightings and the pumps that stopped
records.place: Kuwait Oil Company fields around Umm al-Aish, near the satellite earth station, northern Kuwait
records.explanation: The government’s committee of experts from the Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research ruled out spy aircraft but gave no explanation, and its report was never published. The U.S. embassy reported the stop and restart of the pumping equipment as a Kuwait Oil Company official described it; nothing else about the landing is documented beyond press accounts.
records.shape: A dazzling light; close up, a domed disc the size of a jumbo jet with a red light on top
records.witnesses: Staff of a Kuwait Oil Company pumping station, including an American, and of the nearby satellite station
records.duration: About seven minutes on the ground; the series of sightings ran for five weeks
records.summary: On the night of November 9–10, 1978, according to the Kuwaiti dailies Al-Qabas and Al-Watan, employees of the Kuwait Oil Company and of the satellite station near Umm al-Aish saw a dazzling light come down nearby. Four oil-company workers, one of them an American, went to within about 250 metres and saw a disc as big as a jumbo jet, with a cupola and a red light on top, which stayed on the ground for about seven minutes while telephone and radio links in the area were cut, then rose vertically at great speed. Sightings over the oil fields went on until December 14. The U.S. embassy’s cable to Washington in January 1979, “UFO sightings cause security concern in Kuwait”, reported that the government had set up a committee of experts from the Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research, and that a senior Kuwait Oil Company official said the oil-pumping equipment had shut down automatically during one sighting and started again by itself when the object left, although it could normally be restarted only by hand.
